about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a GAO report to congressional committees evaluating two topics: (1) the fiscal year 2009 overseas master plans, focusing on the changes and challenges they describe, the extent to which they address prior GAO recommendations, and their timeliness; and (2) the status of the Department of Defense's (DOD) master planning efforts for the proposed military buildup on Guam. It is the fifth report on overseas master plans and the second on the Guam military buildup.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's key findings are that while the fiscal year 2009 overseas master plans generally reflect recent changes in U.S. basing strategies and the challenges DOD faces in their implementation, as well as address most of GAO's prior recommendations, DOD provided the plans to Congress in May 2008, 3 months after the February 2008 budget submission. The plans generally address prior recommendations except that the U.S. Pacific Command plan does not provide details of training challenges for the Air Force in South Korea. The report also finds that DOD has developed a basic framework for the military buildup in Guam but has not issued its congressionally required comprehensive master plan that was initially due in December 2006, and which Congress later extended to September 15, 2008. The working-level plan submitted by the 2008 deadline is a onetime requirement and is not considered a comprehensive master plan because the required environmental impact statement and record of decision are not expected to be completed until December 2009 and January 2010, respectively; plans for force composition and facility requirements continue to be refined; and time is needed to address challenges related to funding, operational requirements, and Guam's infrastructure.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report's stated figures include: about 8,000 Marines and their estimated 9,000 dependents from Okinawa, Japan, to Guam by 2014; a 3-month delay in DOD submitting the fiscal year 2009 plans (submitted in May 2008 vs. February 2008 budget submission); approximately 14,000 acres of land returned in Japan; a 76 percent reduction in major U.S. installations in South Korea (from 41 to 10); almost 3,000 acres of land acquisitions in South Korea; over $284 million in facility requirements for the ballistic missile defense program in the Czech Republic; a goal of $1.7 billion in host nation funding for U.S. Central Command; a decrease in Japanese Facilities Improvement Program funding from $1 billion in 1993 to $242 million; the move from Yongsan Army Garrison may not be completed until 2012 (originally expected by December 2008); nearly 20,000 soldiers and their families returned to the United States by U.S. Army Europe; approximately $656 million in residual value and payment-in-kind compensation received by the U.S. government since 1989; an estimated $24.4 billion in the fiscal year 2009 military construction budget, with nearly $1.1 billion (4.7 percent) for overseas locations; a current Guam population of 171,000 expected to increase by an estimated 25,000 active duty military personnel and dependents to 196,000; total cost of all services' realignments on Guam estimated at more than $13 billion; a Marine Corps buildup estimated to cost $10.3 billion; Marine Forces Pacific officials estimating the Marine Corps realignment alone will exceed $15 billion; training ranges in Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands estimated to cost $2 billion; strategic lift operating from Guam estimated to cost an additional $88 million annually; the government of Japan expected to contribute a total of $6.09 billion, with up to $2.8 billion in funds without reimbursement and another $3.3 billion in loans and equity investments; an estimated 500 defense civilians and contractors required to support Marine Corps base operations; a July 2008 study estimating annual construction capacity of approximately $1 billion to $1.5 billion, potentially $2.5 billion with improvements, compared to over $3 billion per year needed by DOD; 15,000 to 20,000 construction workers required, with Guam estimated to meet only 10 to 15 percent of the labor requirement locally; the ballistic missile defense task force expected to consist of approximately 630 soldiers and their estimated 950 dependents; the government of Guam needing $6.1 billion for infrastructure upgrades; and a potential increase in demand on Guam's water and wastewater treatment systems by at least 25 percent.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends two actions for the Secretary of Defense: (1) direct the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology and Logistics to initiate a process of developing global defense posture updates earlier each year so that DOD can provide the congressional defense committees the overseas planning report with the administration's annual budget submission; and (2) direct the Executive Director of the Joint Guam Program Office to provide the congressional defense committees with annual updates of the Guam working-level plan until a comprehensive master plan is finalized and submitted to Congress.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states several unsettled items: DOD has not fully identified funding requirements for the military buildup on Guam, and the $13 billion estimate excludes costs of all other defense organizations; there is uncertainty in the cost-sharing arrangement with the government of Japan, which has stipulated its funds will not be made available until it has reviewed and agreed to specific infrastructure plans; DOD has not fully addressed operational challenges such as providing appropriate mobility support and training capabilities for the Marine Corps on Guam; the potential effects of the military buildup on Guam's community and public infrastructure have yet to be fully addressed; DOD may be asking Congress to fund military construction projects without the benefit of a completed environmental impact statement or a final decision on the full extent of its facility and funding requirements; and no decision has been made on whether to deploy additional forces to Guam under the Grow the Force initiative.

audience.text: The report is addressed to the congressional defense committees.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a GAO report to the Committee on Foreign Affairs of the House of Representatives on electronic waste. It examines the fate of exported used electronics, the effectiveness of regulatory controls over the export of used electronics from the United States, and opportunities for strengthening the federal role in regulating used electronics exports. The report focuses on the Environmental Protection Agency's need for stronger enforcement and more comprehensive regulation of harmful U.S. exports of used electronics.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's own key findings are that a substantial amount of exported used electronics ends up in countries like China and India where they are often handled and disposed of unsafely; current U.S. regulatory controls do little to stem the export of potentially hazardous used electronics because the scope of regulatory control is narrow (only CRTs are regulated), the controls are easily circumvented, and EPA has done little to enforce the CRT rule; and EPA has several options to strengthen the federal role in reducing harmful exports. The GAO found that 43 electronics recyclers were willing to export broken, untested, or nonworking CRTs to fictitious buyers in apparent violation of the CRT rule, and that EPA had not issued its first administrative penalty complaint until July 2008, based on a problem GAO identified.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: EPA reported Americans removed more than 300 million electronic devices from their households in 2006. CRTs contain 4 pounds of lead. Under the CRT rule, exporters could face criminal penalties of up to $50,000 per day of violation and imprisonment of up to 2 years. From mid-February to mid-May 2008, brokers in developing countries made 230 requests for about 7.5 million used CRTs; over 75 percent of the brokers' requests offered $10 or less per unit, and almost half offered $5 or less. A UN University study found the manufacturing phase takes up 80 percent of natural resources used during the life cycle of computers. The U.S. Geological Survey reports 1 metric ton of computer scrap contains more gold than 17 metric tons of ore. A study published in 2007 found children in Guiyu had lead levels more than 50 percent higher than the limit set by the CDC. Shipping rates from the U.S. to West Africa range from $4,000 to $7,000 per 20-foot container, compared to $750 for 40-foot containers to Hong Kong. As of June 2008, 25 companies submitted 47 notices for export of CRTs for recycling. EPA's first administrative penalty complaint sought a maximum civil penalty of $32,500. EPA estimated between 15-20 percent by weight of used and end-of-life electronics are collected for reuse and recycling, with the remaining 80-85 percent disposed of domestically.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The GAO recommends that the Administrator of EPA identify a timetable for developing and implementing a systematic plan to enforce the CRT rule, including enforcement targets, monitoring, follow-up of suspected violations, and prosecution. The report also recommends that EPA develop options to broaden regulations under existing RCRA authority to address exports of used electronic devices that threaten human health and the environment when unsafely disassembled, and cooperate with other federal agencies to improve tracking of exported used electronics. Finally, it recommends that EPA submit a legislative package to Congress for ratification of the Basel Convention.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document notes several unsettled issues. EPA officials stated they had no plans and no timetable for developing the basic components of an enforcement strategy for the CRT rule. EPA's deputy director stated there is no 'hard and fast' rule on how long EPA will rely on outreach as its primary tool. The outcome of two EPA investigations into illegal CRT shipments was pending at the time of the report. The document also notes that some Basel Convention parties argue it regulates international movement of used products for repair, refurbishment, or remanufacture, while the U.S. State Department takes the position it does not, and disagreement persists. EPA's legislative package for Basel Convention ratification has not been submitted to Congress because of other priorities. EPA generally disagreed with the report's recommendations, preferring nonregulatory, voluntary approaches.

audience.text: This report is addressed to the Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Affairs of the House of Representatives, to support its oversight and policy decisions.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report identifies the federal laws, regulations, and mandatory standards that pertain to securing privately owned information technology systems and data in each of the 18 critical infrastructure sectors, and identifies the enforcement mechanisms for each requirement. The report is a summary of a briefing presented to congressional staff and includes the full briefing slides.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's key finding is that at least 34 federal laws, regulations, and mandatory standards exist that pertain to securing privately owned IT systems and data in critical infrastructure sectors; of these, 1 is a law, 25 are regulations, and 8 are mandatory standards. These requirements apply to 10 of the 18 sectors, while 8 sectors (critical manufacturing, defense industrial base, emergency services, government facilities, information technology, national monuments and icons, postal and shipping, and telecommunications) did not identify any such requirements. Each of the 34 requirements has at least one enforcement mechanism, including court injunctions, civil monetary penalties, criminal penalties, and administrative actions.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: At least 34 federal laws, regulations, and mandatory standards, comprising 1 law, 25 regulations, and 8 mandatory standards. The mandatory standards are common to the dams and energy sectors and are counted once. 10 of 18 sectors have applicable requirements; 8 sectors have none. Banking and finance has 17 regulations; the energy sector has 1 regulation and 8 mandatory standards; agriculture and food, chemical, commercial facilities, and nuclear reactors, materials, and waste each have 1 regulation; public health and healthcare has 1 regulation; transportation systems has 2 regulations; drinking water and water treatment systems has 1 law. Enforcement mechanisms include civil monetary penalties up to $1 million per day for banking and finance, up to $25,000 per violation for drinking water, up to $100,000 per day per violation for nuclear reactors, and up to $25,000 per day for chemical; public health and healthcare can impose fines up to $50,000 and imprisonment up to 1 year; transportation systems can impose fines up to $100,000 per violation.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: Not stated in this document.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that there is a possibility that the agencies did not identify all applicable requirements and that GAO did not conduct an independent search for applicable requirements. It also notes that the enforcement mechanisms identified are examples and do not necessarily constitute a complete list. Additionally, the document notes that the risk-based performance standards for the chemical sector had not been finalized or submitted to the Office of Management and Budget for approval and therefore were not yet enforceable.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the Chairman and Chairwoman of the House Homeland Security Subcommittees on Emerging Threats, Cybersecurity, and Science and Technology and on Transportation Security and Infrastructure Protection, and is intended to inform their oversight of critical infrastructure cybersecurity.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report assesses the Federal Aviation Administration's ability to acquire and integrate new air traffic control systems and transition to the Next Generation Air Transportation System (NextGen). It addresses the status and outcomes of FAA's ATC systems acquisition activities, the status of key NextGen planning and transition issues, and the key challenges FAA faces in implementing NextGen.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: Most of FAA's major ATC acquisition programs are being managed within established cost and time estimates since the creation of its performance-based Air Traffic Organization (ATO) in 2004, with 24 major acquisition programs experiencing a cumulative 2.5 percent cost underage and only a 2.7 percent schedule overage. However, FAA does not publicly report changes in cost and schedule baselines for some major ATC acquisitions, which could mask budget increases and schedule delays. JPDO has completed initial versions of three basic planning documents for NextGen, and ATO has reorganized to facilitate the transition, but industry stakeholders have concerns about their lack of impact on planning, the usefulness of planning documents, and the adequacy of FAA's management structure. FAA's ability to implement NextGen will be affected by challenges in research and development, human capital, and infrastructure, including uncertainties about funding and conducting research, a need for new skills and personnel, and the need to reconfigure facilities and expand airport capacity.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: One in four flights faces delays. The U.S. air transportation system handles about 50,000 flights over a 24-hour period. By 2025, air traffic is projected to increase two- to three-fold, equating to about 100,000 to 150,000 flights every 24 hours. In 2007, 27 percent of flights were delayed or canceled. Delays cost passengers, airlines, and the U.S. economy over $40 billion. From February 2004 to June 2008, 24 major acquisition programs experienced a cumulative 2.5 percent cost underage and a cumulative 2.7 percent schedule overage. The acquisitions on which FAA reported performance from 2003 to 2006 collectively exceeded their original budget estimates by approximately $4.4 billion, or over 66 percent. FAA plans to spend roughly $5.4 billion from fiscal years 2009 through 2013 on NextGen development and capital costs. The total federal cost for NextGen infrastructure through 2025 will range from $15 billion to $22 billion. JPDO reported in 2006 that the total cost for NextGen infrastructure may range from $15 billion to $22 billion, with a corresponding cost to system users in the range of $14 billion to $20 billion. NASA's aeronautics research budget declined from about $959 million in 2004 to $511 million in 2008. About $280 million of NASA's proposed $447 million aeronautics research budget proposed for fiscal year 2009 would contribute to NextGen efforts. FAA will spend an estimated $740 million on NextGen-related research and development during fiscal years 2009 through 2013. The administration's proposed budget for fiscal year 2009 requests $56.5 million for FAA research and development to support the integration and implementation of NextGen programs, a substantial increase over the $24.3 million authorized for fiscal year 2008. $111 million for fiscal years 2009 through 2011 may be used for a new FAA program to help close the research and development gap and reduce aviation noise and emissions. FAA plans to invest $180.4 million in human factors research from fiscal year 2009 to fiscal year 2013. FAA estimates it could need 150 to 200 more staff. FAA rated the average condition of 89 terminal facilities as 'fair,' with some rated 'good' and others 'very poor.' FAA estimated that a onetime cost of repair to all of its terminal facilities would range from $250 million to $350 million. FAA simulated the expected capacity enhancement of planned runway improvements and additional capacity gained through NextGen initiatives and found that by 2025, 14 airports will still need additional capacity.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that FAA identify or establish a vehicle for regularly reporting to Congress and the public on the agency's overall, long-term performance in acquiring ATC systems by providing original budget and schedule baselines for each rebaselined program and the reasons for the rebaselining, and report information on the potential effects that any budget increases or schedule slippages could have on the overall transition to NextGen. It also suggests that having the JPDO Director report directly to the FAA Administrator could begin to address JPDO's organizational placement concerns. The document notes that proposed legislation would elevate the Director of JPDO to the Associate Administrator for the Next Generation Air Transportation System, appointed by and reporting directly to the FAA Administrator.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that it is too early to tell if ATO's reorganization addresses concerns about the fragmented management structure for NextGen, since other offices in ATO and FAA continue to have responsibility for parts of NextGen and the division of responsibility is not clear. It also states that it is too early to tell if the FAA-NASA research transition strategy will be effective in addressing NextGen's overall research needs, and that it is too early to tell how the reorganization will affect JPDO's overall role or its ability to coordinate and act as an honest broker among federal partners. The document notes that FAA has not developed a cost analysis or implementation plan for reconfiguring its facilities for NextGen. It also notes that JPDO has not yet determined what NextGen research and development needs to be done first and at what cost. The document indicates that NAPA expects to complete its assessment of FAA's skill needs in September 2008, and that once the right skill set is identified, it may take considerable time to select, hire, and integrate staff.

audience.text: This report is intended for congressional requesters, including the Chairmen and Ranking Members of the House Committee on Science and Technology, the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and the Subcommittee on Aviation Operations, Safety, and Security and the Subcommittee on Aviation, to inform oversight of FAA's acquisition and NextGen transition efforts.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a GAO report (GAO-08-1123) issued September 2008, examining efforts by the Small Business Administration (SBA) and USDA Rural Development to collaborate on rural economic development. It discusses the complementary nature of their loan and business programs, past and current collaborative efforts, and opportunities to improve collaboration, concluding with recommendations for executive action.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's own findings are that the complementary nature of some SBA and Rural Development programs provides a rationale for collaboration; collaborative efforts have been sporadic, initiated mostly by local officials and dependent on established relationships; and opportunities exist to improve collaboration, including making more use of formal agreements, establishing formal incentives, and tracking results.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document does not provide a list or table of numbers, but includes figures such as: fiscal year 2007, 7(a) program provided more than 99,000 loans totaling nearly $14 billion; 504 program provided about 11,000 loans, totaling approximately $6 billion; 7(m) program provided about $19 million in microloans; SBIC program provided over $2.5 billion to more than 2,000 small businesses; B&I program provided over $836 million in loan guarantees; IRP spending totaled about $34 million; RBEG approximately $43 million; RBOG about $7 million; REDLG about $26 million in loans and about $10 million in grants; renewable energy about $48 million in energy loans and $11 million in energy grants, with over $18 million in joint funding; maximum loan amounts: 7(a) $2 million, B&I $25 million; maximum guaranty percentages: 7(a) 85% up to $150,000 and 75% over, B&I 80% up to $5 million, 70% for $5–10 million, 60% over $10 million; SBA processing time 5–7 business days, Rural Development 10–60 days; 68 SBA district offices, 47 Rural Development state offices; about 500 Rural Development field offices; more than 950 SBDC locations; in North Dakota, about one of every four 504 loans in rural communities with populations less than 25,000 used jointly with IRP loans; in fiscal year 2007, the SBIC program provided over $2.5 billion to more than 2,000 small businesses; the 7(a) program sometimes takes as little as 2 business days.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Administrator of SBA and the Secretary of Agriculture take steps to adopt a formal approach to encourage further collaboration in support of common economic development goals in rural areas. Such steps could include establishing and implementing a written agreement; defining and articulating a common outcome; specifying roles and responsibilities; establishing mechanisms to monitor, evaluate, and report on results; and reinforcing accountability for collaborative efforts.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document notes that SBA and Rural Development do not track the results of collaborative efforts, so they cannot share information on benefits; and it notes that the December 2000 MOU was not implemented and had expired, with the agencies not initially in agreement on its status. The document also notes that the effectiveness of certain collaborative efforts (e.g., 'Access to Capital' forums) had not been documented, and that while officials suggested preparing 'success stories' to document benefits, this had not been done.

audience.text: Congressional requesters, specifically the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship and the House Committee on Small Business, and the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Rural and Urban Entrepreneurship.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a GAO report to the Chairman of the Subcommittee on Oversight of Government Management, the Federal Workforce, and the District of Columbia, Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, U.S. Senate, providing an update on the Department of Health and Human Services' (HHS) efforts to define and implement an overall privacy approach for protecting electronic personal health information exchanged within a nationwide health information network.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that since January 2007, HHS has undertaken various initiatives that contribute to developing an overall privacy approach, fulfilling the first part of GAO's recommendation to identify milestones and the responsible entity, and taking important steps in addressing key privacy principles and challenges. However, it also finds that HHS has not fully implemented the recommendation because it has not defined a process for ensuring that all privacy principles and challenges will be fully and adequately addressed, which creates a risk that privacy protection measures may not be consistently built into health IT programs.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report includes a figure from a September 2007 survey sponsored by the Institute of Medicine stating that nearly 60 percent of the respondents did not believe that the privacy of personal medical records and health information was adequately protected.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of Health and Human Services direct the National Coordinator for Health IT to include in the department's overall privacy approach a process for assessing and prioritizing its many privacy-related initiatives and the needs of stakeholders. The agency comments state that HHS is actively pursuing a two-phased process for assessing and prioritizing privacy-related initiatives but neither agreed nor disagreed with the recommendation.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that more work remains and that the department has not defined a process for ensuring that all privacy principles and challenges will be fully and adequately addressed. It also notes that without such a process, some principles and challenges may be addressed extensively, while others may receive inadequate attention, leading to gaps in coverage. The report also notes that recommendations from the Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security Workgroup and the National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics are still under consideration by the Secretary.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report on the significant limitations in first responders' ability to detect and model hazardous releases in urban areas. It covers limitations of CBRN detection equipment, the lack of performance standards and independent testing, the limited capabilities of plume models in urban environments, and data gaps on how CBRN releases affect urban populations.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's key findings are that current CBRN detection equipment has significant limitations: radiological detection equipment cannot predict atmospheric dispersion; chemical detectors are generally inadequate at harmful but sub-lethal levels; and handheld biological detectors are ineffective. DHS has adopted only 4 standards for radiation detection and none for chemical or biological detection equipment, and it does not independently test manufacturers' claims. Plume models, both nonurban and urban, have significant limitations in complex urban settings, and TOPOFF exercises demonstrated problems with coordination and contradictory results. There are also significant gaps in data on how CBRN releases affect heterogeneous urban populations.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: As of October 30, 2007, DHS had adopted 39 total standards, only 4 for radiation detection and none for chemical or biological detection. DHS spending for BioWatch during fiscal years 2005 to 2007 was about $236 million. In the 2001 anthrax attack, 22 persons contracted anthrax disease and 5 died. In one planning scenario, an estimated 6,000 people are killed and economic damages amount to $300 million. An accidental release in Bhopal, India, in 1984 killed approximately 3,800 people. In Graniteville, South Carolina, in 2005, 11,500 gallons of chlorine gas released, causing 9 deaths and at least 529 seeking medical care. Approximately 800,000 shipments of hazardous materials travel daily throughout the United States. Washington state acquired CBRN detection equipment with about $3.2 million of SHSP and UASI grant funds in 2004-2005; Seattle alone spent about $500,000. Connecticut spent about $1.8 million in DHS grants for CBRN detection equipment in 2003-2005. DHS S&T assessed sensitivity of IMS and SAW for V and G nerve agents as approximately 2 ppb to 20 ppb, with limit of detection at 200 ppb to 300 ppb for blister agents. A 2005 detector brand tested by Washington State Radiation Protection officials consistently read only 40 percent of what their current dosimeters read. As of October 2007, RKB included 1,127 certifications and 268 reports of operational suitability testing. ASTM standard E2458 was published in 2006.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of Homeland Security take four actions: (1) reach agreement with other agencies on which agency should have the mission to develop, test, and certify detection equipment for first responders; (2) ensure that manufacturers' claims are independently tested and validated; (3) refine IMAAC's procedures with other agencies, including developing common emergency response practices, refining concept of operations, and delineating qualifying incidents; and (4) work with the federal plume modeling community to accelerate research and development to address plume model deficiencies in urban areas. DHS concurred with these recommendations. DOC suggested an additional recommendation that DHS work with the federal plume modeling community to accelerate research and development, which was included in the final report.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that no agency has the mission to develop, certify, and test radiological detection equipment for first responders to detect atmospheric releases. It notes that DHS does not have an independent testing program to validate manufacturers' claims, and that models have not been adequately validated for urban environments. It states that scientific research on low-level exposure effects is severely lacking, especially for vulnerable populations, and that dose response parameters for the general population do not exist for most chemical warfare agents. The document also states that BioWatch provides a qualitative rather than quantitative assessment, and that the system does not determine how much material was released.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines the extent of undisbursed grant balances in expired grant accounts and the program characteristics and grant management challenges associated with them. It is based on an analysis of data from the Department of Health and Human Services' Payment Management System (PMS), the largest federal civilian grant payment system, and a review of federal regulations, audit reports, and annual performance reports.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report found that during calendar year 2006, about $1 billion in undisbursed funding remained in expired grant accounts in PMS. This balance represented about 1 percent of the total funds made available for all expired grant accounts in PMS during 2006; when focusing only on accounts with undisbursed balances, the amount represented, on average, about 26 percent of the original funding made available. These accounts were associated with thousands of grantees in over 325 different federal grant programs. The report also found that dozens of past audit reports and PARs from agencies such as EPA, HHS, and DOJ suggested that undisbursed balances in expired grant accounts were a long-standing challenge, with common grant management problems including closeouts as a low priority, inconsistent procedures, poorly timed communications, and insufficient compliance or enforcement. Agencies that made concerted efforts to address these problems, such as DOJ's OJP, HHS's NIH, and EPA, were able to improve the timeliness of grant closeouts and decrease the amount of undisbursed funding.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states that PMS handled about 70 percent of all federal grant disbursements in 2006. It found that the quarterly amount of undisbursed funding reported as remaining in expired grant accounts increased from about $600 million in 2003 to about $1 billion during 2006. In 2006, the amount of undisbursed funding in expired accounts with remaining balances represented, on average, about 26 percent of the original funding made available; from March 2003 through March 2005, this percentage ranged between 14 and 16 percent, and from June 2005 through December 2006 it ranged between 24 and 26 percent. For expired accounts with undisbursed balances, the largest amounts were consistently in accounts with funding awards from over $100,000 to $100 million, in project-based awards, and in state organizations. The DOJ OIG reported in 2006 that $172 million in undisbursed funding could have been deobligated. EPA closed out only 37 percent of grants in fiscal year 2005 within 180 days. DOJ's OJP 'Operation Closeout' closed 4,136 grants over 6 months, resulting in over $30 million in deobligated funds, and reduced its backlog from 11,356 to 6,237 expired grants from 2001 to 2005. EPA nearly eliminated its backlog of over 23,000 expired grants by 2005. HHS's 2006 PAR reported more than 64,000 grants with a remaining balance of $1.6 billion eligible for closeout, with 75 percent expired for more than 2 years. In 2005, EPA had a goal of 90 percent grant closure and reported achieving a 95 percent grant closure rate in its 2006 PAR.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Director of OMB instruct all executive departments and independent agencies to take two actions: (1) annually track the amount of undisbursed grant funding remaining in expired grant accounts; and (2) report on the status and resolution of the undisbursed funding in their annual performance plan and in their annual PAR. Because OMB did not commit to implementing the recommendations and did not favor requiring reporting in PARs, the report reiterates its belief that PARs would be appropriate vehicles to address the issue on a governmentwide basis.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report acknowledges that its results for program characteristics cannot be compared to all closed federal grants or all closed grants using PMS, due to the burden of collecting comparable data from eight other federal civilian payments systems or for all closed grants from PMS. The report also notes that each analysis of the quarterly undisbursed funding by program characteristic was an independent assessment and results cannot be combined into a general statement. Additionally, the report states that without comparative data, it cannot be known whether the program characteristics represented a disproportionate share compared to all closed federal grants or all closed grants in PMS. OMB's written comments, included in appendix III, state that it supports the intent of the recommendations but does not commit to implementing them; OMB said it would consider revising its grants management guidance during its regular review and does not favor having agencies report these balances in their PARs.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report (GAO-08-525, issued June 27, 2008) examines federal agency efforts to encrypt sensitive information. It assesses how commercially available encryption technologies can help agencies reduce risks, the federal laws, policies, and guidance for using encryption, and the extent to which 24 major federal agencies have implemented or planned to implement encryption. It is a report to Congressional requesters.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: Most federal agencies had just begun to encrypt sensitive information on mobile computers and devices. While all 24 agencies had initiated efforts, none had completed them. Encryption of stored information lagged behind encryption of transmitted information; agencies reported about 70 percent of laptop computers and handheld devices were not encrypted. None of the agencies had documented comprehensive encryption implementation plans. Weaknesses at six selected agencies included installing and configuring FIPS-validated cryptographic modules, monitoring effectiveness, developing policies and procedures, and training personnel. As a result, federal information may remain at increased risk of unauthorized disclosure, loss, and modification.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In fiscal year 2005, 3,634 incidents were reported to US-CERT; in fiscal year 2006, 5,503; and in fiscal year 2007, 13,029. Of 24 agencies, 8 reported encrypting information on less than 20 percent of laptops and handheld devices, 5 on 20-39 percent, 2 on 40-59 percent, 3 on 60-79 percent, and 6 on 80-100 percent. Of 22 agencies, 10 reported encrypting information on less than 20 percent of portable storage media taken offsite, and 3 on 20-39 percent. Of 17 agencies, 9 reported encrypting sensitive information on less than 20 percent of offsite backup storage media. Of 23 agencies, 18 reported encrypting 80-100 percent of wired Internet transmissions; of 21 agencies, 12 reported encrypting 80-100 percent of wireless transmissions. Of 24 agencies, 18 reported not completing efforts to inventory sensitive information. At six selected agencies, 2 had not installed FIPS-validated modules and 4 had not configured installed technologies per FIPS 140-2; all 6 had not developed or documented policies and procedures; 3 had not adequately trained personnel. At NASA, encryption software was installed on 27 of 29 laptops tested; at USDA, 5 of 52 laptops were not correctly encrypted. HUD had not installed encryption on any laptops; Education had not installed FIPS-validated products on any of 15 tested laptops. A laptop stolen from the Department of Veterans Affairs in 2006 contained personal information of approximately 26.5 million veterans and military personnel.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report makes 20 recommendations. To the Director of OMB: (1) clarify governmentwide policy requiring agencies to encrypt sensitive agency data through additional guidance and/or educational activities; and (2) monitor the effectiveness of agencies' encryption implementation plans and efforts to inventory sensitive information. To the Secretary of Agriculture: (1) establish and implement a mechanism to monitor successful installation and functioning of encryption products; (2) develop and implement departmentwide procedures for encryption key establishment and management; and (3) develop and implement a training program for technical support and end-user personnel. To the Secretary of Education: (1) evaluate, select, and install FIPS 140-compliant products for all encryption needs and document an implementation plan; (2) configure installed FIPS-compliant encryption technologies in accordance with FIPS-validated security settings; (3) develop and implement departmentwide policy and procedures for encryption key establishment and management; (4) develop and implement departmentwide procedures for use of FIPS-compliant cryptography; and (5) develop and implement a training program. To the Secretary of HUD: (1) evaluate, select, and install FIPS 140-compliant products and document an implementation plan; (2) configure installed FIPS-compliant technologies per FIPS-validated settings; and (3) develop and implement departmentwide procedures for use of FIPS-compliant cryptography and for encryption key establishment and management. To the Secretary of State: (1) develop and implement departmentwide policy and procedures for encryption key establishment and management; and (2) develop and implement departmentwide procedures for use of FIPS-compliant cryptography. To the Administrator of GSA: (1) develop and implement departmentwide policy and procedures for encryption key establishment and management; and (2) develop and implement departmentwide procedures for use of FIPS-compliant cryptography. To the Administrator of NASA: (1) establish and implement a mechanism to monitor successful installation and functioning of encryption products; (2) develop and implement departmentwide policy and procedures for encryption key establishment and management; and (3) develop and implement a training program.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: Agencies reported uncertainty regarding the applicability of OMB's encryption requirements. OMB officials stated in April 2008 that 'mobile computers and devices' includes portable storage devices, but this is not clear in any OMB memorandums. The report notes that agencies had not documented comprehensive plans and that OMB did not provide evidence of monitoring agencies' inventory efforts or implementation plans. It also states that until agencies develop and document comprehensive plans, they will have limited assurance of effective implementation and life cycle maintenance. Some agencies had not completed efforts to inventory sensitive information. The report identifies hindrances to implementing encryption at federal agencies in Appendix III.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report on how U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) works with international entities to promote global customs security standards and initiatives, while addressing the challenges that remain in international supply chain security. It covers CBP's actions to develop and implement international supply chain security standards, its efforts to achieve mutual recognition of customs security practices, and the issues anticipated in implementing 100 percent scanning of U.S.-bound container cargo.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: CBP has taken a lead role in developing international supply chain security standards, including the WCO SAFE Framework, which is based on CBP's CSI and C-TPAT programs. CBP works with international partners to implement these standards through capacity-building programs and other collaborative efforts. CBP and international partners have developed different types of mutual recognition, and CBP has engaged in activities to achieve mutual recognition with international partners, including signing mutual recognition arrangements with New Zealand, Jordan, and Canada. Challenges remain in balancing these efforts with the statutory requirement to scan 100 percent of U.S.-bound container cargo, which could adversely impact the implementation of international standards and may provide a lower level of security due to resource constraints.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: As of June 2008, 154 WCO member countries had signed letters of intent to implement the SAFE Framework. The SAFE Framework was adopted in June 2005 by the 173 member customs administrations of the WCO. 11 million oceangoing cargo containers arrived at U.S. seaports in fiscal year 2007, meaning roughly 30,000 oceangoing containers arrived each day that year. As of May 2008, there were over 8,400 C-TPAT members. According to the WCO, as of April 2008, 111 countries were participating in the capacity-building program; as of July 2008, 104 of these countries had completed the first phase, 65 had moved into the second phase, and one was in the third phase. CBP has provided training and assistance to 10 countries in the capacity-building program. In 2002, a simulated scenario estimated seaport closures could result in a loss of $58 billion in revenue to the U.S. economy. 58 foreign seaports participate in the CSI program. As of July 2008, 2 of the 33 countries participating in CSI—Canada and Japan—had decided to station their officials in U.S. seaports. The 9/11 Act requires 100 percent scanning of all U.S.-bound container cargo by 2012.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document does not make specific recommendations for action. It describes statutory requirements, such as the 9/11 Act requiring 100 percent scanning of U.S.-bound container cargo by 2012, and notes challenges that may affect international adoption of standards. DHS provided technical clarifications on a draft of the report, which were incorporated.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that the full impacts of the Secure Freight Initiative pilot program are still unknown. It notes that additional resources needed for 100 percent scanning are unclear, including who will pay for them. It indicates that achieving mutual recognition of customs controls presents a challenge and may not be easily or quickly attained. The document also notes that the results from visits to six seaports cannot be generalized beyond those visited, and the perspectives of foreign officials spoken to cannot be generalized across the wider population of countries.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a GAO report assessing the progress the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has made in implementing recommendations from a 2003 report on the security of radioactive sources, other steps NRC has taken to improve its ability to monitor and track radioactive materials, and the ability of Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to detect radioactive materials at ports of entry on the northern and southern borders and to verify that such materials are appropriately licensed before entering the United States.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that NRC has implemented three of the six recommendations from GAO's 2003 report, including identifying 16 radionuclides of concern, establishing increased security controls, and integrating performance criteria into oversight. NRC has made limited progress on the other three recommendations, including correcting weaknesses in its licensing process, mitigating psychological effects of an RDD, and re-examining general licenses. NRC has taken four steps to improve monitoring and tracking, but three are delayed or not fully implemented. CBP has a comprehensive detection system, but personal radiation detectors are in short supply, and CBP guidance on when to verify licenses was not effectively communicated to the field, leading to some dangerous radioactive materials entering the country without license verification.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: About 2 million sealed sources are licensed for use in the United States. Approximately 22,000 specific materials licenses exist; NRC administers about 3,750, and agreement states administer the rest. NRC has relinquished authority to 35 states. The National Source Tracking System has been delayed by 18 months and is expected to launch in January 2009; expansion to category 3 and largest category 4 sources by July 31, 2009, later revised to at least March 2010. The Web-based licensing system is more than 3 years behind schedule, expected no earlier than late summer 2010. CBP needs approximately 1,500 personal radiation detectors for current officers and approximately 2,000 additional for new hires, leaving a shortfall of about 3,500. Over 90 percent of personally owned vehicles entering at land ports pass through radiation portal monitors. NRC performed preliminary increased controls inspections on approximately 1,100 of the 1,700 licensees subject to the new controls. 22 of 35 agreement states and one of three NRC regional offices have had aspects of increased controls implementation assessed.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Chairman of the NRC take steps to (1) ensure priority attention is given to meeting the January 2009 and summer 2010 target dates for launching the National Source Tracking System, Web-based licensing system, and new license verification system, and (2) complete steps to include all potentially dangerous radioactive sources (category 3 and larger category 4 sources, as well as categories 1 and 2) in the National Source Tracking System as quickly as reasonably possible. The report also recommends that the Secretary of Homeland Security direct the Commissioner of CBP to (1) effectively communicate current CBP guidance to officers at ports of entry regarding when they are required to contact the National Targeting Center to verify the legitimacy of radioactive materials, and (2) take measures to ensure this guidance is being followed. DHS concurred with CBP recommendations and specified steps and a due date of March 31, 2009.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that NRC has not yet determined how to effectively mitigate the potential psychological effects of an RDD, has not yet decided whether certain radioactive sources should be regulated through specific licenses rather than general licenses, and that it is too early to evaluate whether NRC's actions to address licensing vulnerabilities will be successful. The report also notes that the National Source Tracking System and Web-based licensing system have missed numerous milestones and it is uncertain whether current target dates will be met.

audience.text: The report is addressed to the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, U.S. Senate.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) report to congressional committees on tax compliance, specifically examining the problem of businesses owing billions of dollars in unpaid federal payroll taxes. It focuses on three objectives: determining the magnitude of unpaid federal payroll tax debt, identifying factors affecting the Internal Revenue Service's (IRS) ability to enforce compliance and collect these taxes, and determining whether some businesses with unpaid payroll taxes are engaged in abusive or potentially criminal activities. The report was issued in July 2008.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that as of September 30, 2007, over 1.6 million businesses owed over $58 billion in unpaid payroll taxes, including interest and penalties. It states that 70 percent of all unpaid payroll taxes are owed by businesses with more than a year (4 tax quarters) of unpaid taxes, and over a quarter of the debt is owed by businesses that accumulated debt for more than 3 years (12 tax quarters). The report also finds that IRS's collection approach focuses primarily on voluntary compliance, which can allow egregious offenders to continue accumulating debt, and that IRS is not timely in filing liens and assessing Trust Fund Recovery Penalties (TFRPs). It finds that IRS does not measure the effectiveness of its payroll tax collection efforts and that some businesses are engaged in abusive or potentially criminal activities. The report notes that the number of businesses with more than 20 quarters of tax debt more than doubled between 1998 and 2007.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states that as of September 30, 2007, over 1.6 million businesses owed over $58 billion in unpaid payroll taxes. It also reports that IRS processed over 230 million tax returns and collected over $2.7 trillion in taxes in 2007. The annual net tax gap is estimated at nearly $300 billion. IRS estimated that the General Fund had transferred $44 billion to the Social Security and Hospital Insurance Trust Funds over what IRS collected as of November 1, 2007. The report states that 52 percent of the unpaid payroll tax inventory, equal to $30 billion, was classified as currently uncollectible, and that IRS had assigned about $7 billion to revenue officers and about $9 billion was in a queue awaiting assignment. It also notes that from 1998 to 2007, the balance of outstanding payroll taxes in IRS's inventory increased from about $49 billion to $58 billion.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report makes six recommendations to the Commissioner of IRS. Five of the recommendations are for IRS to review or revise its collection policies to provide better monitoring or more detailed guidance on collection actions to be taken against egregious payroll tax offenders and to strengthen its existing collection tools. The sixth recommendation is for IRS to work with states to develop ways of more effectively identifying potential levy sources. The report states that IRS concurred with all six recommendations.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that IRS was unable to determine how many of the less than 700 seizure actions in fiscal year 2007 were taken against payroll tax debtors. It also notes that the estimate of the $44 billion General Fund transfer does not include an estimate for tax debts written off in previous years due to expiration of the statutory collection period. The report states that revenue officers believe the injunctive relief process is too cumbersome to use effectively.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is intended for the Congressional Committees that requested the review of IRS's overall approach to the prevention and collection of unpaid payroll taxes.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines the Department of Energy's Office of Science project management performance, specifically the extent to which it manages projects within cost and schedule commitments, the key factors affecting its performance, and the main challenges it may face in the future.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that of 42 Office of Science projects reviewed from fiscal year 2003 through 2007, more than two-thirds were completed or were under way within original cost and schedule targets. Of 27 completed projects, 24 (89 percent) met original cost targets and 21 (78 percent) were on or ahead of schedule. Of 15 projects still under way as of February 2008, 9 (60 percent) were on track to meet both cost and schedule targets. Only 2 completed projects (7 percent) were both over cost and late. The report attributes this success to strong leadership commitment, management and technical expertise, and rigorous oversight practices, as well as to trimming project scope in some cases, which has raised concerns. The report identifies future challenges from funding and market uncertainties and an aging workforce.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: 42 projects; 27 completed; 15 ongoing; 24 (89 percent) completed within cost; 21 (78 percent) on or ahead of schedule; 5 (19 percent) met either cost or schedule but not both; 2 (7 percent) both over cost and late; 9 (60 percent) ongoing on track; 4 (27 percent) expected to meet cost but not schedule; 2 (13 percent) expected to miss both; $4 billion annual budget; 10 national laboratories; 42 research and development facilities; 12 projects in depth; $2.9 billion (75 percent) total value of 12 projects; 21 percent to 43 percent of workforce eligible for retirement by 2011; $10.9 million (64 percent less than $30.4 million target) Run IIb CDF Detector; $29 million Run IIb D-Zero Detector target; $72 million Center for Nanoscale Materials; $36 million specialized research instruments; $7.2 million HVAC target, $150,000 under; $5.9 million electrical systems upgrade; $5.9 million central supply facility; $168 million Neutrinos at the Main Injector, 23 percent over cost, 17 months late; $58 million SPEAR 3 Upgrade, 18 percent over $49 million target, 14 months late; 91 percent cost increase and 4.5-year delay for NCSX; $531 million U.S. contribution to Large Hadron Collider; $65 million Center for Nanophase Materials Sciences; $53 million to $58 million cost increase for SPEAR 3; $121 million to $188 million cost increase for Large Area Telescope; $37 million to $45 million DOE direct contribution; $15.7 million safety and operational reliability project; $33 million Advanced Light Source expansion; $10.7 million vs $160 million requested for ITER fiscal year 2008; 23,000 contractor staff; 3.6 percent annual growth in science and engineering occupations 1990-2000; almost 15 percent decline in Science staffing since 1999; 5 scientific instruments cut from Spallation Neutron Source.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Energy direct the Director of the Office of Engineering and Construction Management to consider whether other DOE program offices would benefit from adopting selected practices from Science's independent project reviews, such as the frequency and focus of reviews for technically complex projects. It also recommends directing the Office of Engineering and Construction Management to review DOE's project management guidance and consider whether it could be strengthened to help ensure that each project's technical goals, including expected scientific performance and facility requirements, are clearly and sufficiently defined.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that results from the 12-project nongeneralizable sample cannot be used to make inferences about overall performance. It notes that DOE's Inspector General and the Office of Science disagreed over effects of scope changes on technical goals for the Spallation Neutron Source, and that the effect of future budget constraints on the 20-year plan is uncertain. It also notes that the Office of Engineering and Construction Management was considering clarifying project management guidance, potentially by 2009, but had not done so. The document states that no analysis had yet been completed to estimate shortfalls in project management and scientific expertise due to retirements.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the Subcommittee on Investigations and Oversight, Committee on Science and Technology, House of Representatives, and supports congressional oversight of DOE project management.

about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) report on the Department of Energy's (DOE) management of costs and liabilities for its contractors' pension and postretirement benefit plans. It provides information on DOE's analysis supporting its approval of the April 2006 policy changes in Notice 351.1, DOE's liabilities for defined benefit pension and postretirement plans, and DOE's recent actions to manage future costs and liabilities.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's findings include that DOE's documentation supporting Notice 351.1 showed limited evidence that DOE considered policy alternatives, stakeholder sensitivities, or near- and long-term financial and mission impacts. As of September 30, 2007, DOE contractors' defined benefit pension obligations were approximately $27.5 billion and postretirement plan obligations were $10.5 billion, with net liabilities of $69.5 million and $10.3 billion, respectively. Since 2005, DOE awarded 14 contracts with provisions limiting benefits for new employees to no more than 105 percent of comparable organizations. DOE expects these provisions will not substantially affect costs and liabilities for the next 20 to 30 years.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In 2007, contractors contributed $387 million and $334 million to defined benefit pension and postretirement plans, respectively. DOE reported a net liability of $69.5 million for defined benefit pensions and $10.3 billion for postretirement benefits. As of September 30, 2007, benefit obligations were approximately $27.5 billion for pensions and $10.5 billion for postretirement plans, with assets of $27.4 billion and $161.6 million. The net funded status changed from an underfunding of $4.5 billion in fiscal year 2006 to underfunding of $69.5 million in fiscal year 2007 for pensions, and from $5.0 billion to $10.3 billion for postretirement benefits from fiscal years 1997 to 2007.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document does not make recommendations. It states that DOE Order 350.1 requires corrective action plans if benefit value or cost study scores exceed 105 percent of the comparison group, and that recent contracts require new employees' total benefits not exceed 105 percent of the comparison group's average. DOE's policy is to ensure continuation of benefits and reimbursement of related costs for incumbent employees and eligible retirees when contracts are recompeted or expire.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines the extent to which federal benefit programs use electronic payments to disburse benefits, identifies factors agencies consider when implementing or using electronic payments, and identifies potential options for increasing their use, particularly Treasury's actions. It is based on a survey of 42 federal benefit programs and interviews with federal and state agencies, industry representatives, and consumer groups.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: Most federal benefit programs surveyed (34 of 42) used electronic payment methods to distribute benefits, but data limitations prevented determining the extent for most. Direct deposit was the most common method, followed by EBT and Electronic Payment Cards. Among the 18 programs providing data, the percentage of payments made electronically ranged from about 5 to 100 percent; for the 5 largest by dollar value, it was about 54 to 100 percent. Eight programs paid 100 percent electronically, but six of these were education assistance programs paying institutions. Six programs did not use electronic payments and paid by paper check. Agencies consider factors such as financial burden to recipients, program characteristics, costs, and fraud risks. Options to increase electronic payments include new statutory requirements, public outreach, and adapting payment cards. Treasury has initiatives such as the 'Go Direct' campaign and the Direct Express debit card.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Of the 42 programs surveyed, 34 (81 percent) used electronic payments. 18 of 42 programs provided data to compute the percentage of payments made electronically, ranging from about 5 to 100 percent. For the 5 largest of these 18, about 54 to 100 percent of payments were electronic. 8 of 18 programs paid 100 percent electronically. 13 programs provided data on paper check percentage; 9 distributed less than half of the total dollar value by paper check, 4 distributed 100 percent. Treasury disbursed 56 percent of benefit payments electronically in fiscal year 1996, 81 percent in fiscal year 2007, and 81.6 percent as of fiscal year 2008 through January. As of fiscal year 2008 (through January), about 88 percent of Treasury-disbursed payments were benefit payments. Fiscal year 2006 figures include Social Security Retirement Insurance with $418 billion in payments and 33.9 million recipients. The Social Security Disability Insurance program had $77.8 billion and 8.6 million recipients; Supplemental Security Income had $41.5 billion and 7.2 million recipients. The Food Stamp program had $30.2 billion and 26.7 million recipients. Unemployment Insurance had $31.0 billion and 7.5 million recipients. Veterans Compensation for Service-Connected Disability had $28.3 billion and 2.7 million recipients. Federal Pell Grant had $12.9 billion and 5.2 million recipients. Temporary Assistance for Needy Families had $11.3 billion and 4.2 million recipients. Railroad Retirement had $9.9 billion and 577,600 recipients. The WIC program had $5.1 billion and 8.1 million recipients. The 'Go Direct' campaign converted 1.8 million recipients over the last 3 years. The Direct Express pilot had approximately 3,000 participants; 85 percent of users were satisfied, and 88 percent would refer the program to family or friends.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of the Treasury direct the Commissioner of FMS to consider developing a process for conducting outreach to federal agencies on a more regular basis, with the goal of identifying opportunities for increasing the use of electronic payments. For example, Treasury could meet with agency CFOs or their designees and with staff from smaller agencies, on a semiannual or annual basis, to discuss challenges and identify actions to facilitate the transition to electronic payments.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that data limitations did not allow determining the extent of electronic payment use for most programs, in part because states are responsible for disbursing many federal benefit payments and are not required to provide specific payment data to the federal agency. It also notes that some programs were unable to provide data on the percentage of payments made electronically or by paper check. The report discusses challenges such as converting unbanked recipients and reaching new enrollees. It notes that Treasury has no plans to conduct outreach to CFO agencies and other smaller agencies on a regular basis.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the Ranking Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. It is intended to inform Congress about the extent of electronic payment use in federal benefit programs and options for increasing use, supporting oversight and policy decisions.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report on young adults aged 18 through 26 with serious mental illness. It covers the estimated number and demographic characteristics of this population, the challenges they face in accessing appropriate support, how selected states (Connecticut, Maryland, Massachusetts, and Mississippi) provide multidimensional services to them, and how federal agencies support states and coordinate relevant programs.

findings.text: The document's own key findings include: an estimated at least 2.4 million young adults aged 18 through 26 had a serious mental illness in 2006, representing 6.5 percent of the 37 million non-institutionalized young adults in that age range. This estimate is likely low because it excludes certain groups such as the institutionalized. Nearly 90 percent of these young adults had more than one type of mental disorder. Compared to young adults with no mental illness, those with serious mental illness have significantly lower rates of high school graduation (64 versus 83 percent) and continuation into postsecondary education (32 versus 51 percent). About 186,000 young adults with serious mental illness received SSA disability benefits in 2006. The report identifies challenges such as finding tailored services, qualifying for adult programs, and navigating multiple programs. It also describes state programs and federal coordination efforts. The number of young adults with serious mental illness who are homeless or involved in justice or foster care systems was not identified in the document.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines the status of property conveyances and transfers between the District of Columbia and the federal government as directed by Public Law 109-396, including steps taken toward completion, preliminary development, and challenges going forward.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: No property conveyances between the District and the federal government had occurred as of June 6, 2008. All transfers of administrative jurisdiction became effective on December 15, 2006. Several factors have slowed completion of conveyances, including negotiations about cleanup, testing for contamination, disagreements over land, and decision changes about environmental impact statement development for Poplar Point. Limited development has occurred on exchanged properties, and development will take many years to complete. The District and federal government face challenges including cleanup uncertainties, transitioning the Deputy Mayor's Office, and reaching community agreement about development at Poplar Point.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The two largest properties to be conveyed are Poplar Point, a 110-acre property, and Reservation 13, a 67-acre property. The District's structural fiscal imbalance likely exceeded $470 million annually and could have been as high as $1.1 billion. The Master Developer's vision for Poplar Point includes 1.5 million square feet of office space, 3.8 million square feet of residential units, 405,000 square feet of retail space, and 70 acres of parks. Reservation 13 could accommodate about 3,000 new units of housing, nearly 5.5 million square feet of mixed-use development, and more than $80 million in new infrastructure upgrades. The DMPED staff increased from 33 full-time equivalents in September 2007 to 63 in June 2008, expected to grow to 73 by August 2008.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document states that the law authorizing the conveyances mandates that GAO report periodically over a 10-year period about how the properties are used and developed and how this complies with the Anacostia Waterfront Framework Plan. It does not itself recommend or require other actions.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that the extent and location of cleanup required, the cost of environmental cleanup, the determination of responsibility for paying for cleanup, potential complications of relocating U.S. Park Police facilities, and the amount of construction allowed prior to certification are uncertainties. It also states that what qualifies as a 'construction project' is unclear, and that reaching community agreement about how to develop Poplar Point, particularly concerning a soccer stadium, is a challenge.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines the extent to which medically underserved areas (MUAs) lacked health center sites in 2006 and 2007, the types of services provided at those sites, HRSA's oversight of cooperative agreement recipients that assist new access point grant applicants, and the clarity of feedback HRSA provides to unsuccessful applicants.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: In 2006, 47 percent of MUAs nationwide lacked a health center site, with wide variation across census regions and states (e.g., 62 percent in the Midwest, 32 percent in the West). HRSA does not collect data on services provided at individual sites, so the types of services could not be determined. New access point awards in 2007 reduced the number of MUAs lacking a site by about 7 percent, leaving 43 percent lacking a site in 2007, with regional variation remaining. HRSA's oversight of cooperative agreement recipients is limited because it lacks standardized performance measures and is unlikely to meet its policy timeline for comprehensive on-site reviews. HRSA's feedback to unsuccessful applicants was unclear in 38 percent of summary statements from fiscal years 2005 and 2007.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: 47 percent of MUAs lacked a health center site in 2006 (1,600 of 3,421). 62 percent of MUAs in the Midwest and 32 percent in the West lacked a site in 2006. 113 fewer MUAs lacked a site in 2007, resulting in 1,487 MUAs (43 percent) lacking a site. The South census region accounted for 77 of the 113 MUAs. 202 new access point grants were awarded in 2007, with 101 (50 percent) to the South, 47 (23 percent) to the West, 39 (19 percent) to the Midwest, and 15 (7 percent) to the Northeast. 69 percent of High Poverty County competition awards went to the South. 38 percent (26 of 69) of summary statements contained unclear feedback, with 41 distinct examples across criteria.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends four actions for the Administrator of HRSA: (1) collect and maintain readily available data on the types of services provided at each health center site; (2) develop and implement standardized performance measures for training and TA cooperative agreement recipients, including a measure of the number of successful applicants assisted; (3) reevaluate the policy of conducting comprehensive on-site reviews every 3 to 5 years and target resources to recipients most likely to benefit; and (4) identify and take appropriate action to ensure that the discussion of strengths and weaknesses in all summary statements is clear.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that the types of services provided at individual health center sites could not be determined because HRSA does not collect such data. It also states that HHS raised concerns about the exclusion of MUPs, the methodology for proximity of sites, and the utility of the percentage indicator, which the report acknowledges as potential limitations. The report does not settle whether an MUA is sufficiently served by a health center site.

audience.text: This report is intended for the Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations, Committee on Energy and Commerce, House of Representatives, to inform congressional oversight of the Health Center Program.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines U.S. assistance to Palau from 1995 to 2009 under the Compact of Free Association, including direct assistance, federal services, road construction, and discretionary federal programs; Palau's accountability for these funds; and prospects for economic self-sufficiency. It also provides information on amendments to the compacts with the Federated States of Micronesia and the Republic of the Marshall Islands as relevant to Palau's 2009 compact review.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: U.S. aid to Palau in 1995-2009 is expected to exceed $852 million, with compact direct assistance accounting for $411 million, compact federal services for about $25 million, compact road construction for $149 million, and discretionary federal programs for $267 million. Palau made progress in financial accountability by improving timeliness and reliability of financial statements but has persistent internal control weaknesses and limited capacity to address them; Interior's oversight has been limited. Palau's prospects for economic self-sufficiency depend on continuing U.S. assistance, trust fund withdrawals, fiscal reform, and private sector growth. A compounded annual return of at least 8.1 percent will allow $15 million annual withdrawals for 35 years; the trust fund had earned 9 percent from 1995 through March 2008, but market volatility makes depletion possible after 2016.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document states: U.S. assistance 1995-2009 projected at more than $852 million; compact direct assistance $411 million (48%); compact federal services $25.3 million (3%); compact road $149 million (17%); discretionary federal programs $266.7 million (31%). For 1995-2006, top five agencies' expenditures: Education $56.2 million (28%), HHS $51.6 million (25%), Interior $39.1 million (19%), DOD $23.8 million (12%), DOT $12.9 million (6%), Other agencies $19.8 million (10%). Trust fund balance $160.775 million as of March 2008; compounded return 9% from inception to March 2008; required return for 35-year withdrawals 8.1%; required return for perpetuity 8.6%; annual returns ranged from 24% in 1998 to negative 12% in 2002; probability of depletion by 2030 close to 26%, by 2044 approximately 46%; in 2009, compact direct assistance $13.3 million, discretionary federal programs $11.9 million, other donor assistance $17.8 million, domestic revenue $43.6 million, total potential revenues $86.6 million; net fiscal impact of expiring direct assistance about $3.3 million annually (less than 4% of 2009 revenues); compact federal services cost estimated at almost $1.6 million in 2009; inflation will reduce value of annual withdrawal by about half by 2044.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of the Interior direct the Office of Insular Affairs to (1) formally consult with the government of Palau regarding Palau's financial management challenges and (2) target future technical assistance toward building Palau's financial management capacity.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document notes that the trust fund consultations required every 5 years were not held, and that the annual economic consultations were informal and not held annually. It also states that the impact of the expiration of the federal programs and services agreement on discretionary federal programs is uncertain, and that forecasts of future trust fund returns are subject to considerable uncertainty. The document does not settle whether Palau will achieve economic self-sufficiency.
