about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a GAO report comparing the amount of Title IV financial aid awarded to veteran students and nonveteran students, how higher education institutions allocate Title IV aid among these groups, and how federal agencies and schools provide information to veterans about Title IV aid. It is based on a performance audit conducted from February through June 2008 and includes data from academic year 2005 to 2006 for Pell Grants and Stafford Loans, and 2003 to 2004 for campus-based aid.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report found that overall, veteran students received similar amounts of Title IV aid as nonveteran, independent students, but when including Chapter 30 GI benefits, veterans received more total federal aid. Laws and regulations largely dictate how schools allocate Title IV aid, but five of the eight schools interviewed used their limited flexibility to allow veterans to be eligible for larger amounts of certain types of Title IV aid. Federal agencies and schools provide the same information on Title IV aid to all students, but some schools reach out to veteran students, and there are recent federal efforts to inform veterans about Title IV aid.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In fiscal year 2007, Education provided $82 billion in Title IV financial aid to 11 million students and their families. VA awarded about $2 billion in Chapter 30 education benefits to more than 300,000 veteran students in fiscal year 2007. In academic year 2005 to 2006, the average Pell Grant for veteran students was $2,322 and for nonveteran independent students was $2,482. The average subsidized Stafford Loan for veterans was $2,082 and for nonveterans was $2,109. The average unsubsidized Stafford Loan for veterans was $2,959 and for nonveterans was $2,945. Campus-based aid for veterans averaged $1,450 and for nonveterans $1,300 (estimates, not significantly different at the 95% confidence level). The average Chapter 30 GI benefit for veterans was $9,306. Veterans received on average 6 percent less in Pell Grants in academic year 2005 to 2006. The 2005 to 2006 monthly Chapter 30 GI benefit rate was $1,034 for veterans with 3 or more years of service attending full-time. The maximum Pell Grant in 2005 to 2006 was $4,050, and the maximum subsidized Stafford Loan for first-year undergraduates was $2,625.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document does not make explicit recommendations. It is a report to the Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, and it notes that the report does not address how federal financial aid amounts for reservists compare with other students and suggests this 'may warrant further inquiry.'

unsettled.text: The report states that it does not address how the federal financial aid amounts reservists receive compare with other students, which may warrant further inquiry given the increasing number of reservists called to active duty and important differences in their receipt of GI benefits. It also notes that the findings from interviews with eight schools cannot be generalized beyond those schools.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report assesses the Department of Defense's implementation of its National Security Personnel System (NSPS), focusing on the extent to which DOD has incorporated internal safeguards for fairness, effectiveness, and credibility, and on employee attitudes toward NSPS. It covers DOD's actions, survey findings, and recommendations for improvement.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that while DOD has taken steps to implement internal safeguards, the implementation of some safeguards could be improved, specifically predecisional internal safeguards, reasonable transparency, and meaningful distinctions in employee performance. It also finds that although NSPS employees are positive about some aspects, DOD does not have a plan to address generally negative employee perceptions identified in surveys and discussion groups. DOD has phased in over 182,000 civilian employees into NSPS as of May 2008.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Over 182,000 civilian employees phased into NSPS as of May 2008; 58,000 comments received during design; 100 focus groups sponsored in 2004; 95 employees in contractor workshops; approximately 14 percent (71,000 employees) responded to web-based questionnaires; 10-hour training for transitioning employees; 80 percent of fourth estate employees trained; 18 hours basic training for managers/supervisors; 24 hours pay pool panel training; 26 or more hours for human resource practitioners; 10 hours for employees; $158 million November 2005 cost estimate; approximately $143 million estimated implementation costs for fiscal years 2009-2011; 43 percent of NSPS employees agreed pay raises depend on performance vs 25 percent of all other DOD employees; 67 percent in May 2006 agreed performance appraisal fair vs 52 percent in May 2007; 40 percent in May 2006 believed NSPS positive effect vs 23 percent in 2007; rating distributions: DOD-wide 57.0% at rating 3, 36.1% at 4, 5.1% at 5; pay pools visited: 60% or more at rating 3 in 9 pay pools.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that DOD (1) require a third party to perform predecisional demographic and other analysis as appropriate for pay pools, (2) require overall final rating results to be published, (3) encourage pay pools and supervisors to use all categories of ratings as appropriate, and (4) develop and implement a specific action plan to address employee perceptions of NSPS ascertained from DOD's surveys and employee focus groups.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that it was unable to determine whether final rating distributions were meaningful because specific knowledge of employee performance within pay pools was lacking. It also notes that survey responses were fairly evenly distributed across 'disagree,' 'agree,' and 'neither' responses, so the overall trend is unknown and whether the negative movement will continue in future years is unclear. It also states that the findings from discussion groups are not generalizable to the entire population of DOD civilians.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines the roles of major national voluntary organizations in providing mass care and other human services in response to large-scale disasters, the steps they have taken since Hurricane Katrina to strengthen their capacity, what is known about their current capabilities, and the remaining challenges they face. It covers five organizations: the American Red Cross, The Salvation Army, the Southern Baptist Convention, Catholic Charities USA, and the United Way of America, with a focus on four high-risk metropolitan areas.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that voluntary organizations are major providers of mass care and other services in large-scale disasters, but their collective capabilities have not been fully assessed. A worst-case disaster would likely overwhelm their current sheltering and feeding capabilities without government and other assistance. The Red Cross's role changed from primary to support agency under the 2008 National Response Framework, but the Catastrophic Incident Supplement still describes it as the primary agency, and no interim agreement or timeframe for updating the Supplement exists. Voluntary organizations have taken steps since Katrina to expand coverage and strengthen service delivery, but challenges remain, including shortages of trained personnel, limited financial resources, and coordination with government.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The Red Cross raised more than $2.1 billion following the 2005 hurricanes; The Salvation Army raised $325 million; Catholic Charities USA raised $150 million; the United Way raised $28 million; the Southern Baptist Convention raised about $20 million. During Hurricane Katrina, the Red Cross provided more than 52.6 million meals and snacks, opened more than 1,300 shelters across 27 states, and provided 3.4 million overnight stays. The Southern Baptist Convention provided more than 14.6 million meals, and The Salvation Army provided 3.8 million articles of clothing. The Red Cross projects a FY2008 operating budget deficit of about $150 million. It reduced staff by about 1,000 in early 2008. The Red Cross's estimated cost for ESF-6 staff is $7 million annually, and it requested $10 million total, including $3 million for integrating nongovernmental sector mass care services. In the four metro areas, the Red Cross has identified 386 shelter facilities in Washington, D.C.; 623 in New York; 341 in Los Angeles; and 65 in Miami. The Red Cross has identified 50,000 potential shelter facilities nationally and has sheltering supplies to support up to 500,000 people. The Red Cross's local sheltering capacity in Los Angeles is 84,000 people under optimal conditions. DHS estimates a major earthquake could necessitate shelter for as many as 300,000 people. Red Cross estimates for worst-case disasters include 564,113 people needing shelter in Southern California, 300,000 in Washington, D.C., 605,000 in New York City, and 328,646 in the Gulf Coast; feeding needs include 2.5 million people in Southern California, 4 million in New York City, and 657,292 meals per day in the Gulf Coast.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Homeland Security direct the Administrator of FEMA to: (1) establish a time frame for updating the mass care section of the Catastrophic Incident Supplement so it is consistent with ESF-6 changes and no longer requires the Red Cross to direct federal resources, and in the meantime develop an interim agreement with the Red Cross documenting its role and responsibilities; (2) take steps to better incorporate voluntary organizations' capabilities into assessments of mass care capabilities, such as FEMA's GAP Analysis, and broaden the assessment to include feeding capabilities outside shelters; and (3) clarify Homeland Security Grant Program funding guidance so it is clear that voluntary organizations and local VOADs are among those eligible to be subgrantees.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that FEMA does not currently have a time frame for updating the Catastrophic Incident Supplement, and there is no interim agreement documenting FEMA's and the Red Cross's understanding of the Red Cross's role as a support agency. It also states that initial assessments have not fully captured the collective capabilities of major voluntary organizations, and that assessments are hindered by a lack of standard terms and measures. The report notes that the effect of the Red Cross's staffing cuts remains to be seen, and it is too soon to tell how they will affect service delivery and coordination. It also notes that the Red Cross's community partnership strategy is not tracked nationally, so the exact number of new agreements is unknown.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report assesses the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) progress in addressing lessons learned from its first Cyber Storm cyber attack simulation exercise, identifies the lessons DHS learned from that exercise, and presents key participants' views of their experiences during the second Cyber Storm exercise. It is addressed to the House Committee on Homeland Security and the Subcommittee on Emerging Threats, Cybersecurity, and Science and Technology.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: DHS identified eight lessons from Cyber Storm I, which involved improving interagency coordination groups, contingency planning and risk assessment, integration of incidents across infrastructures, access to information, coordination of response activities, strategic communications and public relations, processes/tools/technology, and the exercise program. DHS identified 66 activities to address these lessons; as of the report's writing, 42 were completed, 1 was reported completed but not validated, 16 were ongoing, and 7 were planned. Key activities remained incomplete, and DHS had not set completion dates for ongoing activities. Cyber Storm II participants observed progress but also continued challenges, many similar to those from Cyber Storm I, including clarifying roles and responsibilities and improving classified information handling.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Cyber Storm I cost about $3.7 million and was conducted in February 2006. It involved eight federal departments and three agencies, three states, four foreign countries, 11 information technology companies, 7 electric companies, 1 banking and finance company, 2 airlines, and over 100 public and private agencies, associations, and corporations. Cyber Storm II cost about $6.4 million and was held in March 2008. It involved 18 federal agencies, 9 states, 10 information sharing and analysis centers, 5 foreign countries, and over 40 industry representatives. DHS identified 66 activities; 42 were completed, 1 reported but not validated, 16 ongoing, and 7 planned. DHS listed 121 activities to address lessons 1 through 8, but 55 repeated prior activities. After the draft report, DHS completed additional items, raising the percentage of corrective actions completed to over 70 percent (from over 66 percent).

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Homeland Security direct the Assistant Secretary for Cybersecurity and Communications to ensure the scheduling and completion of the corrective actions addressing lessons learned during Cyber Storm I before conducting the next Cyber Storm exercise. DHS concurred with this recommendation.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that DHS had not identified completion dates for activities reported as ongoing, and that until DHS schedules and completes its remaining activities, the agency risks conducting subsequent exercises that repeat lessons learned during the first exercise. It also notes that many challenges noted during Cyber Storm II were similar to ones identified during the first exercise. DHS stated that end dates are not applicable for many remaining corrective actions because they are long-term, dependent on outside stakeholders, or ongoing, but GAO found most remaining activities could be associated with a time frame.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is for the House Committee on Homeland Security and the Subcommittee on Emerging Threats, Cybersecurity, and Science and Technology, to inform oversight of DHS's cybersecurity exercise program and corrective actions.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) report to congressional committees on the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) risk-based methodology for allocating grant funds, specifically the Homeland Security Grant Program (HSGP), which includes the State Homeland Security Program (SHSP) and the Urban Areas Security Initiative (UASI). It assesses the methodology used for fiscal year 2008 and compares it with fiscal year 2007, evaluating the reasonableness of the risk analysis model and noting limitations in its vulnerability measurement. The scope covers grant allocation processes, risk analysis model components (threat, vulnerability, consequences), changes to urban area boundaries, and recommendations for improvement.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's key findings are that DHS's risk-based methodology is generally reasonable for allocating funds within a given fiscal year, but the vulnerability element of the risk analysis model has limitations that reduce its value. DHS assigned a constant vulnerability score of 1.0 across all states and urban areas, ignoring variations in vulnerability. The primary change from fiscal year 2007 to 2008 was the shift to metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) for defining urban area boundaries, which altered risk rankings and expanded the eligible urban areas to 60. The model's results were less sensitive to changes in assumptions in 2008 than in 2007, especially regarding Tier 2 eligibility.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document states that since 2002, DHS distributed almost $20 billion in federal funding. In fiscal year 2007, DHS provided approximately $1.7 billion through HSGP and planned to distribute approximately $1.6 billion in fiscal year 2008. In fiscal year 2007, the six Tier 1 UASI grantees were allocated approximately $410.8 million (55 percent of available funds), and the 39 Tier 2 grantees received approximately $336.1 million (45 percent). In fiscal year 2008, the top seven Tier 1 grantees were allocated approximately $429.9 million (55 percent of available funds), and the 53 Tier 2 grantees received approximately $351.7 million (45 percent). The change to MSAs resulted in an increase of almost 162,000 square miles across the total area of urban area footprints.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of DHS instruct FEMA, I&A, and NPPD to formulate a method to measure vulnerability in a way that captures variations across states and urban areas, and apply this vulnerability measure in future iterations of the risk-based grant allocation model. It notes that FEMA and I&A concurred with this recommendation, and that FEMA, NPPD and I&A provided technical comments.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that DHS did not measure vulnerability for each state and urban area, but assigned a constant score of 1.0, which reduces the value of the vulnerability element and ignores geographic differences. It also notes that earlier iterations of the model (fiscal year 2006) attempted to measure vulnerability but that the current model does not. The document mentions that DHS acknowledged in fiscal year 2006 it did not have sufficient data on all infrastructures to know specific vulnerabilities, and that fully developing this capability would require substantial time and resource investment.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This document is addressed to the Subcommittee on Homeland Security of the Committee on Appropriations in both the United States Senate and the House of Representatives, and is intended to support congressional oversight of DHS's grant allocation methodology.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines the extent to which federal agencies use the authorities of the Defense Production Act of 1950 (DPA), specifically Titles I, III, and VII, and assesses agencies' response to reporting requirements on the economic impact of foreign offsets. The review focuses on use since the 2003 reauthorization in the areas of defense, energy, domestic emergency and disaster response and recovery, and critical infrastructure.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that DOD is the primary user of DPA authorities, while civilian agency use has been limited. DOD routinely exercises Title I priorities and allocations authority, placing priority ratings on almost all of its contracts for industrial resources, which number approximately 300,000 annually. In contrast, civilian agencies generally have not used the Title I authority and most differ from DOD in deciding when to apply it, placing ratings on a case-by-case basis after an issue affecting delivery has been identified, potentially causing delays during emergencies. The report also finds that civilian agencies responsible for responding to domestic emergencies in civil transportation, health resources, and food and agriculture resources have not developed and implemented policies or guidance to use the Title I authority. Other DPA authorities have been used exclusively for defense needs or have not been triggered by recent events. The report also finds that agencies have taken steps towards fulfilling their offset reporting requirements to Congress, but the type of data collected by the Department of Commerce limits the analysis of the economic effect of offsets.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: DOD places priority ratings on almost all of its contracts for industrial resources, which number approximately 300,000 annually. DHS reported that it has authorized or endorsed to the Department of Commerce the use of priority ratings 15 times since 2003. The most recent annual report on offsets noted that its analysis does not include the potential effects of nearly $1 billion of technology transfer, training, and overseas investment offset transactions, representing nearly 24 percent of average annual offset transactions. Documentation was requested for only two weapon systems from each of the 13 U.S. prime contractors. The survey had a less than 40 percent response rate. 84 percent of the value of export contracts involving offsets submitted by prime contractors are for the aerospace industry. DHS reported that because of the time needed to use the Title VII voluntary agreement authority it could take 21 to 50 days to establish a voluntary agreement following a disaster. Commerce reported that since late 2003, it has taken approximately 180 actions to provide Special Priorities Assistance. In 2002, DOT obtained a priority rating to support the procurement of approximately 1,800 Explosives Detection Systems (EDS) machines. DOD has proposed increasing the statutory limitation on actions under Title III from $50,000,000 to $200,000,000. Title III projects have dedicated funds ranging from $88,000 to approximately $164 million. Table 2 lists specific project funds, including $163.91 million for Radiation Hardened Microelectronics Capital Expansion and $449.3 million as the total for Title III projects.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretaries of Agriculture, Health and Human Services, and Transportation, in consultation with the Department of Commerce, develop and implement a system for using the priorities and allocations authority for food and agriculture resources, health resources, and civil transportation respectively. It also recommends that the Secretaries of Agriculture, Energy, Health and Human Services, Homeland Security, and Transportation consider, in advance of an emergency, approving programs and placing priority ratings on contracts for items that are likely to be needed in an emergency. Additionally, it recommends that the Secretary of Commerce update regulations to, for example, request more specific industry information from prime contractors that would improve the assessment of the economic effects of offsets.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that the interagency team chaired by DOD has reached consensus with foreign nations that the adverse effects of offsets exist, but not yet on best practices to address them. It also notes that participating nations in the interagency working group noted that it will be difficult and time-consuming to produce a preliminary statement of best practices, which was established as a goal for the latter half of 2008. The report states that the National Commission on Offsets was to provide a final report with areas for additional study and concrete policy recommendations, but the final report and recommendations were never produced due to the 2001 change in the presidential administrations. The report also notes that Commerce's employment analysis relies on aggregated defense aerospace data, which do not include other defense sectors nor delineate between subsectors of the aerospace industry.

audience.text: This report is addressed to the Congressional Committees, including the Committees on Armed Services and Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs of the United States Senate and the Committees on Armed Services and Financial Services of the House of Representatives.

about.text: This is a GAO report on the Trans-Sahara Counterterrorism Partnership (TSCTP), examining the distribution of funds from 2005 through 2008 and the types of activities supported, as well as the program's implementation, including the extent to which it has been guided by a comprehensive, integrated strategy.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The key agencies distributed the majority of the obligated and committed resources to the Sahel region in 2005 through 2008, supporting diplomacy, development assistance, and military activities. Several challenges have hampered implementation, including the lack of a comprehensive, integrated strategy; disagreements between State and DOD about authority over DOD personnel; fluctuation in funding for USAID activities in Mali; and a lack of common mechanisms for measuring outcomes.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: About $353 million in obligations and commitments for TSCTP from the program's inception through 2008. About 74 percent of approximately $230 million obligated in 2005 through 2007 went to the Sahel region, about 3 percent to the Maghreb region, and about 8 percent to the sub-Saharan region, with the remaining 15 percent for regional assistance. For 2008, approximately $123 million was committed, with about half expected to go to the Sahel countries. In 2005 through 2007, funds distributed to Sahel countries included $23 million for Chad, $31 million for Mali, $18 million for Mauritania, and $37 million for Niger. In 2008, commitments were $9 million for Chad, $6 million for Mali, $6 million for Mauritania, and $7 million for Niger. In 2005 through 2007, funds distributed to Maghreb countries were $1 million for Algeria, $3 million for Morocco, and $0 for Tunisia; in 2008, commitments were $6 million, $6 million, and $1 million respectively. In 2005 through 2007, funds distributed to sub-Saharan countries were $9 million for Senegal and $3 million for Nigeria; in 2008, commitments were $3 million and $5 million respectively. In 2005 through 2007, $22 million was for regional assistance; in 2008, $10 million. An additional $147 million was obligated for program support costs. For State and USAID TSCTP activities by country and year, figures include for Chad: $2,780,000 in 2005, $2,990,000 in 2006, and $2,895,000 in 2007; for Mali: $2,330,000, $550,000, and $13,570,000; for Mauritania: $2,620,000, $58,000, and $6,200,000; for Niger: $3,220,000, $4,340,000, and $5,372,000; for Algeria: $417,876, $0, and $0; for Morocco: $1,550,000, $463,381, and $382,423; for Tunisia: $0, $32,836, and $0; for Nigeria: $0, $0, and $1,260,000; for Senegal: $397,000, $1,160,000, and $3,970,000; and for regional: $5,000,000, $0, and $3,650,000.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of State work through the Director of Foreign Assistance, who serves concurrently as USAID Administrator, to develop a comprehensive strategy for TSCTP in conjunction with the Secretaries of Defense and the Treasury, the U.S. Attorney General, and the heads of any other participating agencies. It also recommends that the Secretaries of State and Defense issue joint guidance regarding DOD personnel temporarily assigned to conduct TSCTP activities in the partner countries.

It also notes that disagreements between State and DOD regarding authority over DOD personnel have not been resolved, and that the agencies are working to develop indicators to assess outcomes. The report mentions that a classified annex is planned.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines the Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board's (CSB) response to prior GAO and inspector general (IG) recommendations concerning its investigative gap, data quality, human capital, and accountability and management problems, and assesses the merits of the current IG oversight approach versus alternatives. It is a performance audit conducted from October 2007 to May 2008, mandated by the fiscal year 2008 Consolidated Appropriations Act, and summarizes briefings to congressional subcommittees.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: CSB has not fully addressed several critical recommendations, and problems in governance, management, and oversight persist. Specifically, CSB has not fully responded to key recommendations related to investigating more accidents that meet statutory requirements, improving the quality of its accident data, resolving human capital problems, and ensuring accountability and continuity of management. The investigative gap persists; in fiscal year 2007, CSB investigated less than 1 percent (5 of 920) of accidents notified. Data quality problems continue, including inaccuracies and incompleteness in the accident-screening database. Human capital problems persist, with more employees leaving than hired in fiscal years 2006 and 2007, and retention challenges. Accountability and management problems continue, as CSB operates without a permanent chief operating officer. In GAO's view, independent oversight from an existing IG remains the most effective way to help CSB address its continuing problems, provided the arrangement is made permanent and funding is provided to the IG for the function.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: CSB received notification of approximately 900 chemical accidents in calendar year 2007, with 31 serious or fatal events. CSB received an appropriation of $9.4 million for fiscal year 2008 and had 39 staff as of January 30, 2008. Since fiscal year 2001, three IGs have made 32 recommendations. Using fiscal year 2002 data, the DHS IG reported in fiscal year 2004 that CSB deployed to 4 of 294 accidents that met statutory criteria. In fiscal year 2007, CSB received notifications of 920 chemical accidents; approximately 35 of these included at least one fatality, and CSB investigated 1 of these. NTSB's budget is approximately 8 times CSB's budget, and NTSB investigates 250 times as many accidents. In fiscal year 2006, NTSB investigations totaled 1,521 and budget was $75.9 million; CSB investigations totaled 6 and budget was $9.1 million. In a subset analysis, GAO found at least five accidents (about 6 percent) where fatalities were not correctly recorded, and seven accidents (about 4 percent) where injury data were missing. In fiscal year 2006, CSB reprogrammed compensation funds of $627,891; in fiscal year 2007, $407,383. CSB has not paid a retention bonus since September 2002. In fiscal year 2006, CSB recorded 822 accidents, deployed to 9, investigated 6, and investigated 5 of 38 accidents with fatalities. In fiscal year 2007, CSB recorded 920 accidents, deployed to 8, investigated 5, and investigated 1 of 35 accidents with fatalities. CSB's fiscal year 2009 request was $10.6 million and 47 staff; fiscal year 2000 request was $12.5 million and 60 staff. Prior appropriations: fiscal year 2008 $9.4 million and 39 staff; fiscal year 2006 $9.2 million and 41 staff; fiscal year 2004 $8.2 million and 40 staff; fiscal year 2000 $8.0 million and 27 staff. CSB currently obtains its financial and information security audits for about $60,000 a year.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO recommends that the chairman of the Chemical Safety Board: (1) develop a plan to address the investigative gap and request the necessary resources from Congress to meet CSB's statutory mandate or seek an amendment to its statutory mandate; (2) consider using the work of other entities, such as government agencies, companies, and contractors (subject to an assessment of the quality of their work), to a greater extent to maximize the board's limited resources; (3) improve the quality of its accident-screening database by better controlling data entry and periodically sampling accident data to evaluate their consistency and completeness; (4) publish a regulation requiring facilities to report all chemical accidents, as required by law, to better inform the agency of important details about accidents that it may not receive from current sources; (5) consider reinstating the position of chief operating officer, with delegations of responsibility for establishing performance goals, holding program managers accountable for meeting those goals, and demonstrating improvement in the agency's ability to meet its statutory mandates over time; and (6) use the Strategic Management of Human Capital portion of the President's Management Agenda to provide criteria for developing a comprehensive human capital plan, with input from investigators, that includes specific objectives and performance measures to improve accountability for results and to assist the agency in its goal of improving its human capital and infrastructure. Congress may wish to consider amending CSB's authorizing statute or the Inspector General Act of 1978 to permanently give EPA's Inspector General the authority to serve as the oversight body for the agency, and providing the EPA IG with appropriations and staff allocations specifically for the audit function of CSB via a direct line in the EPA appropriation. CSB generally concurred with four of six recommendations and disagreed with two, and disagreed with both matters for congressional consideration.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: GAO notes that CSB has not explained the basis for its interpretation of its authorizing statute, and GAO continues to believe the current law is clear that investigations are required for all accidental releases that result, or have the potential to result, in a fatality, serious injury, or substantial property damage. The report also states that GAO did not evaluate the quality of CSB's investigative products issued to date, or the quality and effectiveness of its reports, recommendations, and promotion of preventive actions, because those evaluations were outside the scope of the mandate. GAO also did not conduct a detailed evaluation of the oversight arrangements for the other 53 federal entities for comparison with CSB. Additionally, GAO recognized shortcomings with the current EPA IG's oversight relationship, including that the arrangement is not permanent and that EPA IG officials have no plans to conduct future program evaluations of CSB.

audience.text: This report is addressed to the Congressional Committees, specifically the House and Senate Appropriation Subcommittees on Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies, to inform their oversight and funding decisions regarding CSB.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a GAO report on the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation's (PBGC) contracting activities. It assesses the role of contracting in PBGC's mission, the steps taken to improve its acquisition infrastructure and strategic approach, and the improvements in contract oversight, and makes recommendations for improvement.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: Contracting plays a central role in helping PBGC achieve its mission and address unpredictable workloads. PBGC is taking steps to improve its acquisition infrastructure, but its Procurement Department is not yet part of PBGC's strategic decision-making process. PBGC has made improvements to contractor oversight and has begun to implement performance-based contracting, which offers potential for better outcomes but also creates new challenges.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: PBGC insures pensions for more than 44 million workers in over 30,000 employer-sponsored defined benefit plans. In fiscal year 2007, roughly 611,000 beneficiaries received over $4.1 billion in benefit payments. PBGC's current workforce consists of about 800 federal employees and utilizes the services of about 1,500 contract employees. PBGC had an accumulated deficit of $14 billion for its single-employer program as of September 2007. PBGC's contract spending increased from $122 million in fiscal year 2000 to $297 million in fiscal year 2007. PBGC's budget increased from $165 million in fiscal year 2000 to $398 million in fiscal year 2007. Contracting represented 71 percent of PBGC's appropriated budget during this period. PBGC had 791 contract employees in fiscal year 2000 and over 1,500 in fiscal year 2007. Federal employees increased from 763 in fiscal year 2000 to 811 in fiscal year 2007. Contract employees peaked in fiscal year 2006 at 1,768, falling to 1,502 in fiscal year 2007. PBGC manages $68 billion of assets. The case processing cycle takes an average of 3 years or more. PBGC has awarded less than $150 million in service contract dollars in fiscal year 2008. Only six of its contracts currently are performance based, representing a yearly cost of approximately $30 million. PBGC is in the process of awarding an additional $20 million in performance-based contracts for field benefit administration offices. While only 2 of 12 staff in the contract specialist series were certified as of February 2007, by January 2008, 9 of the 12 staff had been certified. PBGC had 88 percent more transactions on average and 40 percent more contract dollars on average than the other four agencies in the May 2007 staffing study.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Director of PBGC revise its strategic plan and, in drafting the human capital strategic plan, reflect the importance of contracting and PBGC's use of contractors, project its vision of future contractor use, and better link staffing and contracting decisions at the corporate level. It also recommends including the Procurement Department in agency-wide strategic planning, ensuring the Procurement Director sits on three strategic teams, broadening the May 2007 staffing study, including detailed plans for contract support, assessing contract information needs, and developing metrics for the annual performance plan. To improve contract management, it recommends providing comprehensive training on performance-based contracting, developing practices to ensure accountability for contract monitoring, and ensuring future contracts measure performance in terms of outcomes and provide incentives.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that PBGC has not yet fully integrated its contracting function at the corporate level, and it is still too early to tell what the effect of the new policies will be. It also notes that the strategic approach has not yet been developed and that implementation of performance-based contracting may present challenges.

audience.text: This report is intended for the Congressional Requesters, specifically the Committee on Finance and the Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions of the United States Senate, and other interested parties.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report (GAO-08-877) examines how the Department of Defense (DOD) and military services have managed the acquisition of tactical radio systems, specifically focusing on changes in planned investments over the past five years, the reasons for these changes, and the challenges ahead. It compares planned versus actual spending on legacy radios and the Joint Tactical Radio System (JTRS), and assesses whether DOD has a strategy to balance near-term and long-term requirements.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that DOD investments in tactical radios shifted dramatically over fiscal years 2003-2007, with actual spending exceeding plans by more than double—from about $3.2 billion planned to about $8.3 billion actual—shifting from JTRS procurement to legacy radio procurement. This change was due to delays in JTRS development and increased demand for legacy radios from combat operations and force restructuring. DOD lacks a comprehensive strategy for balancing future tactical radio investments, as previous migration plans are outdated and the waiver/notification process has been ineffective. The report also notes that JTRS faces significant technology, cost, and security challenges that could delay further fielding.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document states that DOD spent an estimated $12 billion on tactical radio development and production over the last 5 years. Planned spending for fiscal years 2003-2007 was about $3.2 billion (including $2.93 billion for JTRS and $0.24 billion for legacy radios), while actual spending was about $8.3 billion (including $2.54 billion for JTRS and $5.72 billion for legacy radios). Legacy radio spending was about $5.7 billion, approximately 24 times the planned amount. The Army spent $4.1 billion on legacy radios, including $2.3 billion on SINCGARS and $1.8 billion on handheld and manpack radios; the Marine Corps spent $1.6 billion. Supplemental funding supplied an estimated 90 percent ($5.5 billion out of $6.1 billion) of legacy radio funding for the Army and Marine Corps. The JTRS Ground Mobile Radio production decision was delayed from 2005 to 2010. The estimated cost to develop JTRS increased from about $3.5 billion to almost $6 billion through fiscal year 2011. A legacy vehicle radio costs about $20,000, while a JTRS replacement is estimated at up to 10 times more. The Army's SINCGARS acquisition objective increased from about 232,000 units in fiscal year 2002 to more than 526,000 in 2007. The Army bought 244,780 SINCGARS between 2003 and 2007. The Marine Corps rifle company radio count increased from 9 to about 225. The Army's planned SINCGARS request in fiscal year 2008 was overstated by $1.7 billion, with 170,756 requested versus 56,000 needed. The JTRS Ground Mobile Radio quantity was reduced from 108,086 to 86,512 (20 percent decrease); Handheld, Manpack, and Small Form Fit was reduced from 328,514 to 95,551 (71 percent decrease); and Airborne, Maritime, and Fixed Station was reduced from 17,007 to 11,040. The cost to retrofit JTRS into four Naval aircraft is estimated at $868 million. A single-channel JTRS radio costs about $2,000 (preliminary) versus $8,700 for the small form factor C radio. The report also cites a Nunn-McCurdy unit-cost breach for the Ground Mobile Radio program declared in November 2007, reflecting a 24 percent increase above the 2002 baseline.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Defense develop a comprehensive strategy and implementation plan for tactical radio investments, based on operational architectures, that assesses and prioritizes capabilities, sets funding bounds, lays out a migration and fielding plan, and identifies contingencies for delays with JTRS. It also recommends reinvigorating the tactical radio notification/waiver process to provide department-wide insight into legacy and interim radio procurements.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that DOD's migration plan has not been updated and remains outdated. The Army has not yet developed a JTRS migration plan. Service input for a new fielding plan has not been linked to operational architectures and lacks detail on requirements and funding priorities. The JTRS program still faces technology hurdles, size and power constraints, and security architecture issues. It is uncertain whether these technical challenges can be overcome until major test and evaluation events in the next few years. The report also notes that the Army overstated its SINCGARS request by $1.7 billion in fiscal year 2008.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is intended for the Subcommittee on Air and Land Forces of the House Committee on Armed Services, and also for DOD leaders, to inform oversight and decision-making on tactical radio investments.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report to congressional requesters assessing the status of the federal courthouse construction project for the L.A. District Court, the effects of delays on costs and court operations, and the options for the project's future. It details the project's history, cost escalation, and lack of consensus among stakeholders.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that the estimated costs to house the L.A. District Court have nearly tripled from about $400 million to over $1.1 billion, that the project has been delayed by 8 years, and that there is no consensus on how to proceed. It also finds that the delays have caused operational, space, and security problems to persist or worsen, and that GSA has developed eight proposals since 2000, with three still under consideration requiring additional appropriations ranging from $282.1 million to $733.6 million.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Congress appropriated approximately $400 million for the project: $35.25 million in FY 2001, $50 million in FY 2004, and $314.4 million in FY 2005. GSA has spent $16.3 million designing the courthouse and $16.9 million acquiring and preparing the site; about $366.45 million remains. The cost estimate for a 41-courtroom courthouse in May 2004 was about $400 million; current estimates exceed $1.1 billion. Each day of additional delay costs about $54,000. The 36-courtroom option would cost $733.6 million more, the 20-courtroom option $301.5 million more, and the existing-buildings option $282.1 million more. The current space deficits are 133,838 square feet for court, chamber, and support space; 3,292 for probation; 6,165 for district clerk's office; and 9,635 for jury assembly; projected 2011 deficits are 197,613, 6,426, 25,696, and 9,650 square feet respectively.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document does not recommend any specific option. It states, 'We are not advocating any of these options. Our intent is to identify current options so that Congress and stakeholders can evaluate them.'

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that there is no consensus on how to proceed, that all options require congressional approval and additional appropriations, and that some cost estimates may not be viable. It also notes that the L.A. Court opposes the 20-courtroom and existing-buildings options, and that the process is deadlocked.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report assesses whether the Department of the Navy is effectively implementing information technology management controls on the Navy Enterprise Resource Planning (Navy ERP) program, focusing on the program's first increment. It evaluates controls in architectural alignment, economic justification, earned value management, requirements management, and risk management.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that DOD has implemented key IT management controls on Navy ERP to varying degrees of effectiveness. One control (requirements traceability) was fully implemented; important aspects of other controls were not. Specifically, compliance with DOD's federated business enterprise architecture was not sufficiently demonstrated; the investment was economically justified but with estimating limitations; earned value management was not effectively implemented; and a risk management process was defined but not effectively implemented for all risks. These weaknesses have contributed to the program being more than 2 years behind schedule and costing about $570 million more than originally envisioned.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Navy ERP's first increment is expected to cost approximately $2.4 billion over its 20-year life cycle, with about $8.6 billion in estimated benefits. Deployment is more than 2 years behind schedule and about $570 million more than originally envisioned. The life cycle cost estimate was about $1.87 billion in fiscal year 2003, $1.99 billion in fiscal year 2004, and $2.44 billion in fiscal year 2007. Approximately $400 million was spent from fiscal year 2004 through fiscal year 2007 on the first increment, with about $200 million planned for fiscal year 2008. The cost to complete just the budgeted development work for all three releases is about $844 million, with a most likely overrun of about $152 million. As of May 2008, the program had not completed about $24 million in scheduled work.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report makes recommendations to the Secretary of Defense aimed at addressing cost and schedule estimating, EVM, and risk management weaknesses. It does not make recommendations for addressing architecture compliance weaknesses because of other work more broadly focused on that control.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that DOD's federated BEA and DON's enterprise architecture are not sufficiently defined to permit thorough compliance determinations. It also notes that benefit estimates were not subject to uncertainty analysis, and the cost estimate lacks historical comparable data and a reliable schedule baseline. The report states that the program lacks an integrated master schedule including all three releases, and that an integrated baseline review has not been performed on any release. It also notes that not all known risks are captured in the risk inventory.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is intended for the Subcommittee on Readiness and Management Support, Committee on Armed Services, U.S. Senate, and supports oversight of DOD business systems modernization.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines how states with Gulf Opportunity Zones (GO Zones) allocated and utilized four federal tax incentives provided under the GO Zone Act of 2005: tax-exempt private activity bonds, low-income housing tax credits, tax credit bonds, and additional advance refunding bonds. It covers the allocation processes, the extent of use, and challenges faced by Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Texas.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: As of mid-June 2008, the three eligible states had allocated about 87 percent of the $14.9 billion in GO Zone tax-exempt private activity bond authority, and the five eligible states awarded 95 percent of the $330 million in LIHTCs. Bonds have been issued for about half of the awarded allocation authority, reflecting 44 percent of the total. The states used GO Zone bonds for a wide range of purposes including housing, utilities, manufacturing, retail, and hotels. Few planned LIHTC units were in service as of April 2008, but state officials anticipate they will be in service by the end of 2010. GO Zone LIHTC units will address 17 percent and 45 percent of rental housing units with major or severe damage in Louisiana and Mississippi, respectively. Louisiana and Mississippi exhausted their tax credit bond authority issuing $300 million, while Alabama did not issue them. The three states used 16 percent of the advance refunding authority.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: $14.9 billion in tax-exempt private activity bond authority; $330 million in LIHTC allocation; $350 million in GO Zone tax credit bonds; $7.9 billion in additional advance refunding bonds. As of mid-June 2008, allocations: Alabama 88%, Louisiana 89%, Mississippi 84% of private activity bond authority. Bonds issued: 44% of total allocation authority. LIHTC awards: 95% of $330 million as of April 2008. Planned LIHTC units: Alabama 3,259, Florida 226, Louisiana 11,787, Mississippi 9,301, Texas 398. In-service units: Alabama 68, Florida 0, Louisiana 2,156, Mississippi 328, Texas 0. GO Zone LIHTC units will address 17% of rental housing units with major or severe damage in Louisiana and 45% in Mississippi. Tax credit bonds issued: Louisiana $200 million, Mississippi $100 million. Advance refundings issued: Alabama $599 million (53% of allocation), Louisiana $483 million (11%), Mississippi $169 million (8%).

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document does not make explicit recommendations. It states that state officials provided technical comments that were incorporated, and the report was mandated by Congress to study state and local practices. It does not call for specific actions.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document notes limits: data on major or severe damage to rental housing were not available for every GO Zone parish and county in Louisiana and Mississippi, or for Alabama, Florida, or Texas. It states that due to differences in bond type reporting, aggregate use by categories across states was not quantified. It also notes that the extent to which monitoring policies have been followed was not assessed since few units were in service. It identifies challenges including reduced credit availability, declining tax credit values, and difficulties in identifying eligible debt for advance refundings.

audience.text: This report is addressed to the Committee on Finance, U.S. Senate and the Committee on Ways and Means, House of Representatives, to inform them on state and local practices in allocating GO Zone tax incentives.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO follow-up audit report on the Department of Veterans Affairs' (VA) progress in strengthening controls over information technology (IT) equipment. It assesses VA's actions on prior recommendations and the effectiveness of current internal controls to prevent theft, loss, or misappropriation of IT equipment, including results of a VA-wide physical inventory and statistical tests at four case study locations.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: VA has completed action on 10 of 12 recommendations from GAO's July 2007 report and 4 of 6 property-related recommendations from the July 2004 report. VA's 2007 departmentwide physical inventory initially identified approximately 79,000 missing IT equipment items, and as of May 15, 2008, about 62,800 items remained missing, of which over 9,800 could have stored sensitive information. GAO's statistical tests at four case study locations identified 50 missing items, of which 34 could have stored sensitive information. Estimated control failure rates for missing items ranged from 1 percent at Puget Sound HCS to 12 percent at VA headquarters. Other failures included blank serial numbers (up to 59 percent at North Texas HCS), incorrect user organization (up to 91 percent), incorrect user location (up to 46 percent), and recordkeeping errors (up to 41 percent). Weaknesses were also found in controls over hard drives in the disposal process and physical security at IT storage locations.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Approximately 79,000 missing IT equipment items initially; approximately 62,800 recorded IT equipment items could not be located as of May 15, 2008; over 9,800 could have stored sensitive information. GAO identified 50 missing items, of which 34 could have stored sensitive information. Estimated control failure rates: missing items: Puget Sound HCS 1%, Boston HCS 3%, North Texas HCS 6%, VA headquarters 12%; blank serial numbers: North Texas HCS 59%, Boston HCS 17%, Puget Sound HCS 1%, VA headquarters 1%; incorrect user organization: North Texas HCS 91%, Boston HCS 60%, Puget Sound HCS 76%, VA headquarters 12%; incorrect user location: North Texas HCS 46%, Boston HCS 17%, Puget Sound HCS 14%, VA headquarters 33%; recordkeeping errors: North Texas HCS 9%, Boston HCS 41%, Puget Sound HCS 9%, VA headquarters 4%. Population sizes: North Texas HCS 12,172, Boston HCS 15,706, Puget Sound HCS 11,474, VA headquarters 34,735. Missing items from 2007 inventory: North Texas HCS 5,309 as of Dec 31, 2007; 5,308 not located as of May 15, 2008; Puget Sound HCS 1,383; 1,269; Boston HCS 3,663; 3,226; VA headquarters 1,595; 1,314. Missing items that could have stored sensitive information: North Texas HCS 3,351, Puget Sound HCS 443, Boston HCS 725, VA headquarters 608. VA-wide totals: 62,880 total missing items, 9,866 open Reports of Survey items that could have stored sensitive data, including 7,993 desktop computers, 104 main frame systems, 1,364 laptop computers, 170 personal digital assistants, 244 other. As of May 15, 2008, VA had over 43,000 items on open Reports of Survey.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of Veterans Affairs require the CIO, with support from medical centers and VA headquarters organizations, to take five actions: (1) Review property inventory records and confirm that all IT equipment, regardless of the organizational equipment inventory listing, is identified in the property system. (2) Establish and implement a policy requiring development of standardized naming classifications for IT equipment—including item name, manufacturer, and model—for recording IT equipment into local property inventory systems. (3) Develop a list of medical equipment with data storage capability that should be considered as IT equipment for inventory control purposes. (4) Develop a procedure for identifying hard drive serial numbers with both the property identification numbers and serial numbers of host computers. (5) Revise the definition of IT storage locations in VA's Handbook 0730/1 to include informal IT storage locations, such as OIT work rooms, and require these locations to be included in physical security inspections.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document does not settle what sensitive information resided on missing equipment or when it was lost, so notifications to potentially affected individuals could not be made. It also notes that VA could not determine whether missing items were lost or stolen, and that the numbers of missing items could be higher because not all IT equipment items were included in the departmentwide inventory (e.g., medical equipment with data storage capabilities, and items not accounted for in the OIT equipment inventory listing). The document states that VA officials could not tell the quantity of IT equipment items that were not included in the four case study populations.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a July 31, 2008, Government Accountability Office (GAO) report to congressional requesters on information technology (IT) project rebaselining across 24 major federal agencies. It addresses the extent of and primary reasons for rebaselining major IT projects funded for fiscal year 2008 and whether agencies have sound rebaselining policies.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own findings, based on a GAO survey and analysis, are: An estimated 48 percent of the federal government's major IT projects have been rebaselined, with 51 percent of those rebaselined at least twice and about 11 percent rebaselined four or more times. The most commonly cited reasons for the most recent rebaselining were changes in project requirements, objectives, or scope (55 percent) and changes in funding stream (44 percent). Examples show rebaselining can result in significant cost and schedule changes, such as the Coast Guard's Rescue 21 system, which is projected to have cost increases of 184 percent and schedule delays of 5 years. While all 24 major agencies have established rebaselining policies, none are fully consistent with best practices from GAO's Cost Assessment Guide, and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) has not issued guidance specifying what elements these policies should include.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The federal government planned to spend about $70 billion on IT projects during fiscal year 2008 on 778 major projects. The survey of a random sample of 180 projects achieved a 99% response rate. An estimated 48 percent of major IT projects have been rebaselined. Of rebaselined projects, 51 percent were rebaselined at least twice and about 11 percent were rebaselined 4 times or more. The most commonly cited reason for rebaselining was changes in project requirements, objectives, or scope--55 percent. Another frequently cited reason was changes in funding stream--44 percent. The U.S. Coast Guard's Rescue 21 system is projected to experience cost increases of 184 percent and schedule delays of 5 years after rebaselining. For the National Polar-orbiting Operational Environmental Satellite System, original cost was $7000 million, cost after rebaseline(s) was $12500 million, a dollar change of $5500 million (79 percent), original completion date was 2018, completion date after rebaseline was 2026 (8-year delay). For Navy Enterprise Resource Planning, original cost was $1993 million, cost after rebaseline(s) was $2445 million, a dollar change of $452 million (23 percent), original completion date was Jun. 2011, completion date after rebaseline was Aug. 2013 (2.2-year delay). For FAA Standard Terminal Automation Replacement System, original cost was $940 million, cost after rebaseline(s) was $2770 million, a dollar change of $1830 million (195 percent), original completion date was Oct. 2005, completion date after rebaseline was Dec. 2007 (2.2-year delay). For FAA Wide Area Augmentation System, original cost was $1001 million, cost after rebaseline(s) was $3340 million, a dollar change of $2339 million (234 percent), original completion date was Aug. 1999, completion date after rebaseline was Dec. 2008 (9.3-year delay). For US Coast Guard Rescue 21, original cost was $250 million, cost after rebaseline(s) was $711 million, a dollar change of $461 million (184 percent), original completion date was 2006, completion date after rebaseline was 2011 (5-year delay). The report also states that 79 percent, 96 percent, and 88 percent of agency policies fully or partially addressed describing reasons for rebaselining, requiring management review, and requiring that the rebaselining process be documented, respectively. Describing the process for developing the new baseline was not addressed in 46 percent of policies, and requiring validation of the new baseline was not addressed in 54 percent of policies.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Director of OMB issue guidance for rebaselining policies that would include a minimum set of key elements, taking into consideration the criteria used in this report. It also recommends that each of the heads of the 24 major agencies direct the development of comprehensive rebaselining policies that address the weaknesses identified.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that OMB has acknowledged it has not established specific criteria to evaluate agencies' earned value management policies, which include rebaselining. The report also states that agencies' policies vary in part because OMB has not issued guidance specifying what elements these policies are to include. Without comprehensive policies, the report concludes that new baselines may be inaccurate and fail to provide necessary transparency to agency officials, OMB, and other oversight organizations.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is for the Subcommittee on Federal Financial Management, Government Information, Federal Services, and International Security of the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, United States Senate, to support its oversight of federal IT project management.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report assesses DOD's logistical planning for the reposturing (drawdown) of U.S. forces from Iraq, focusing on the retrograde of materiel and equipment. It covers planning efforts, command roles, and key issues that need to be addressed.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that DOD's reposture planning began in fall 2007 but was uncoordinated until May 2008, and is based on three key assumptions. It also finds that DOD has not clearly established roles and responsibilities for managing retrograde, leading to confusion and inefficiencies. Additionally, several issues—such as hazardous materials management, contractor reposturing, and infrastructure capacity—need attention.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: As of April 26, 2008, approximately 149,400 DOD contractors; as of July 1, 2008, approximately 147,400 U.S. troops. As of March 2008, theater provided equipment totaled approximately 173,000 major end items worth approximately $16.5 billion. As of May 2008, approximately 582,000 pieces of equipment worth about $15.5 billion; more than 60,000 materiel containers; over 127,000 short-tons of ammunition. At least $3.5 billion in contractor-managed government-owned property; $3.37 billion under LOGCAP. 211 wash racks (81 at Camp Arifjan, 130 at Kuwait Naval Base; 100 useable). 311 installations. Equipment cleaning times: larger vehicles 40 to 80 hours, smaller 4 to 8 hours. 177 pieces of rolling stock idle on May 16, 2008; over 2,100 non-rolling stock items idle.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Defense, in consultation with CENTCOM and the military departments, take steps to clarify the chain of command over logistical operations in support of the retrograde effort, and correct the incompatibility weaknesses in data systems used for in-transit visibility. It also suggests that Congress may wish to direct DOD to include specific reposturing details in its briefings.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that the pace and overall extent of reposturing have yet to be determined. It states that the effect of CENTCOM's June 2008 action designating ARCENT as having operational control over the 401st and 402nd Army Field Support Brigades has not been evaluated. It also notes that time and costs for base closures are difficult to estimate without a bilateral agreement, and that several home station issues need further exploration.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a GAO report to the Ranking Member of the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs on the Department of Veterans Affairs' (VA) progress in reducing underutilized and vacant real property. It addresses the extent of reduction, the cost of maintaining such property, VA's use of legal authorities to reduce it, and challenges VA faces in minimizing underutilized and vacant property. The report contains recommendations for executive action by the Secretary of Veterans Affairs.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's key findings are that VA reduced underutilized space in its buildings from 15.4 million square feet in fiscal year 2005 to 5.6 million square feet in fiscal year 2007, but vacant space remained relatively unchanged at approximately 7.3 million square feet in fiscal year 2007. The report estimates that VA spent $175 million in fiscal year 2007 operating and maintaining underutilized and vacant space at its medical facilities. It also finds that VA does not track the overall effect of its various legal authorities on space reductions or the financial and nonfinancial benefits from agreements. Additionally, the report identifies ongoing challenges to reducing underutilized and vacant property, including building location, high repair costs, competing stakeholder interests, and legal restrictions.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: VA has over 32,000 acres of land and over 6,200 buildings on approximately 300 sites. Underutilized space decreased from 15,374,292 square feet in fiscal year 2005 to 9,795,006 in 2006 and 5,591,257 in 2007. Vacant space was 7,367,340 square feet in 2005, 7,635,489 in 2006, and 7,297,407 in 2007. The number of vacant buildings decreased from 684 in 2006 to 482 in 2007. GAO estimated that VA spent $175 million operating and maintaining underutilized and vacant space in fiscal year 2007. about.text: This GAO report (GAO-08-954, issued July 2008) assesses the progress the Department of Defense (DOD) and the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) have made in developing electronic health record systems that allow for full interoperability of personal health care information between the departments, steps taken to comply with federal interoperability standards, and efforts to set up the joint interagency program office required by the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2008. It is the first in a series of semi-annual reports mandated by that act.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's findings are that DOD and VA have established and implemented mechanisms to achieve interoperable sharing of some, but not all, electronic health information. Pharmacy and drug allergy data for shared patients are exchanged in computable form, while other data such as microbiology results, cytology reports, and chemistry and hematology reports are shared in viewable form. Not all electronic health information is shared, for example, immunization records, data on exposure to health hazards, and psychological health treatment records. The departments have agreed upon numerous common standards. The joint interagency program office is still in its early stages: leadership positions are not permanently filled, staffing is incomplete, and facilities have not been designated. The implementation plan for the office is still in draft form, with some dates for activities not determined. The report concludes that without a fully established program office and a finalized plan, the departments may be challenged in meeting the September 2009 deadline.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document states that as of June 2008, outpatient pharmacy and drug allergy data were being exchanged on more than 18,300 shared patients. The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2008 required the joint interagency program office to implement interoperable systems by September 30, 2009. Schedules and benchmarks for the office were due by February 28, 2008, and the draft implementation plan was dated April 25, 2008. Permanent staff for the office are expected to number about 30. $4.94 million was requested to fund the office for fiscal year 2008, and funding requirements of $6.94 million for fiscal year 2009 were submitted in June. The departments expect to appoint a permanent Director and Deputy and begin recruiting staff by October 2008, with the office fully operational by December 2008. VA stated it plans to appoint the Deputy Director by October 2008 and hire permanent staff by December 2008. By October 31, 2008, the departments expect to identify milestones and timelines for requirements for interoperable health records. Of 52 milestone dates for Interoperability II, 19 are yet to be determined. In 2006, the Certification Commission certified the first 37 ambulatory electronic health record products, and has certified over 100 products to date. Under the Consolidated Health Informatics initiative, agencies agreed to endorse 20 sets of standards. AHLTA version 3.3 was conditionally certified in April 2007.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretaries of Defense and Veterans Affairs give priority to fully establishing the Joint Interagency Program Office by expediting efforts to put in place permanent leadership, staff, and facilities, and to make the necessary decisions to finalize the draft implementation plan.

unsettled.text: The document does not settle whether the DOD/VA Information Interoperability Plan will be effective, stating that GAO has not yet performed an assessment of it, and noting that it could improve prospects if it includes essential elements. It also notes that the departments are unable to track the number of shared patients currently receiving care, so the number for whom data could potentially be shared is unknown. The information to be covered by Interoperability II enhancements has not yet been fully defined. It also states that the departments expect to receive recommendations on possible approaches for a joint inpatient health record system at the end of July 2008, and no decision has been made.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) report on the Veterans Health Administration (VHA), a component of the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), examining whether the design of VHA's internal controls over the use of miscellaneous obligations was adequate for fiscal year 2007. The report, GAO-08-976, was issued September 11, 2008, and is 43 pages long. It was requested by the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations of the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's key findings are that VA policies and procedures were not designed to provide adequate controls over the use of miscellaneous obligations with respect to oversight by contracting officials, segregation of duties, and supporting documentation. The report states that these control design flaws increase the risk of fraud, waste, and abuse at the 129 VHA stations using miscellaneous obligations in fiscal year 2007. It also finds that new guidance issued in May 2008 offered some improvement but did not fully address the three problem areas, and that VA attorneys had not reviewed these policies. The findings are the document's own, based on GAO's review of IFCAP data and case studies at three VHA medical centers.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In fiscal year 2007, VHA used miscellaneous obligations to record over $6.9 billion against its appropriations. The IFCAP data shows nearly 132,000 miscellaneous obligations with a total value of nearly $9.8 billion were created. Almost $3.8 billion (55.1 percent) was for fee-based medical and dental services, and another $1.4 billion (20.4 percent) was for drugs, medicines, and hospital supplies. In the third quarter of fiscal year 2007, $4.8 billion (56 percent) of the reported $8.6 billion in procurements was done using miscellaneous obligations. VA received appropriations of over $77 billion in fiscal year 2007, including over $35 billion for health care. VHA operated more than 1,200 sites of care in fiscal year 2007. The number of patients treated increased by 47.4 percent from 3.8 million in 2000 to nearly 5.6 million in 2007. In the case studies, 42 miscellaneous obligations were reviewed, with a total dollar value of $36,045,896. In 30 of these 42 obligations, one official performed two or more key functions; in 13 of the 42, the same official performed three functions; in 2 instances one official performed all four functions. Over 88,000 (69 percent) of 127,070 miscellaneous obligations did not include vendor information, accounting for over $5 billion of the $6.9 billion in recorded miscellaneous obligations. The analysis identified 145 miscellaneous obligations for over $30.2 million that appeared to be used for items such as passenger vehicles, furniture, and equipment.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, in conjunction with VA's Office of General Counsel, develop and implement policies and procedures consistent with federal appropriations law and internal control standards that: establish a process for the review of miscellaneous obligations by contracting officials, including requiring appropriate documentation that the review has occurred; segregate duties for (1) creating, approving, and recording miscellaneous obligations; (2) the certification and payment of invoices; and (3) the receipt of the resulting goods or services; document the purposes, vendors, and contract numbers of miscellaneous obligations; and establish an oversight mechanism to ensure that these control policies and procedures are fully and effectively implemented. The document also states VA concurred with these recommendations.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that GAO could not reconcile IFCAP miscellaneous obligations to VA's Financial Management System because FMS does not identify the method used to obligate funds. The document also states that the case study results were not generalizable to the universe of VHA medical centers, and that the 42 obligations reviewed could not be projected to the overall population. It also notes that GAO did not verify that VHA officials were properly following the fee schedule for non-VA physicians, and that GAO's work was not specifically designed to identify fraudulent purchases or estimate their full extent.

audience.text: This report is addressed to the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations, Committee on Veterans' Affairs, House of Representatives, to support their oversight of the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Veterans Health Administration.

It covers DOD's steps to inform reservists of their obligations to provide advance notice to employers, DOD's outreach initiatives, and whether there has been a reduction in hiring of reservists since September 11, 2001.

DOD has used ESGR as its focal point in establishing a strategic approach to promote positive working relationships between reservists and their employers, but it does not measure the efficiency and effectiveness of these efforts. An estimated 79 percent of those responding to a 2006 DOD SOFS said that they had been briefed on USERRA at least once. According to the 2007 SOFS, an estimated 76 percent of reservists had received an informal alert notice; of those, an estimated 77 percent received notice of 30 days or more. It also notes that the results of focus groups and structured interviews were not generalizeable because they were based on nonprobability samples. The report notes that DOD does not collect data that would enable it to gauge the effectiveness of its efforts to inform reservists of their obligations to provide advance notice to employers.
