about.text: This GAO report examines the Transportation Security Administration's (TSA) requirements for domestic air carriers to conduct watch-list matching for domestic flights against the No Fly and Selectee lists, and the extent to which TSA has assessed air carriers' compliance with those requirements. It covers TSA's security directives, oversight inspections, the 2008 revision to the No Fly List security directive establishing a similar-name matching baseline, and TSA's expectation that Secure Flight will be the ultimate solution.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: TSA issued two security directives (one for the No Fly List and another for the Selectee List) that delineate requirements related to air carrier watch-list matching, including similar-name matching. Prior to April 2008, TSA's requirements were broad and allowed air carriers discretion in comparing name variations, leading to uneven effectiveness. In April 2008, TSA revised the No Fly List security directive to specify a baseline capability for similar-name matching, and planned a similar revision for the Selectee List. Until a January 2008 special emphasis inspection, TSA had conducted limited testing of air carriers' similar-name-matching capability; the inspection found no air carrier was successful in identifying matches involving all types of name variations. TSA conducted 1,145 watch-list-related inspections in fiscal year 2007, finding compliance in 1,133 (99 percent) of them.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The 14 air carriers interviewed accounted for approximately 70 percent of all passengers that boarded domestic flights in 2005. As of January 2008, nine principal security inspectors were responsible for assessing domestic air carriers' compliance with the No Fly and Selectee list security directives. For fiscal year 2007, there were 72 domestic air carriers to which the security directives applied. As of June 2008, there were 681 transportation security inspectors responsible for 459 commercial airports. In fiscal year 2007, TSA conducted 1,145 inspections of air carriers' compliance with watch-list-related requirements; 1,109 at airport locations and 36 at corporate security offices. The 1,145 inspections covered 60 of the 72 domestic air carriers, and TSA found compliance in 1,133 (99 percent) of the inspections. Available records referenced name-matching tests in 6 of the 36 principal security inspector inspections and 55 of the 1,109 transportation security inspector inspections.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document does not make recommendations. It states that TSA has taken corrective actions and has plans, including revising the No Fly List security directive in April 2008 to establish a baseline capability for similar-name matching, planning to revise the Selectee List security directive similarly, and intending to deploy Secure Flight beginning in January 2009. It also states that TSA plans to issue new inspection guidance, and that efforts are still underway.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that it is too early to determine the extent to which TSA will assess air carriers' compliance with watch-list-matching requirements moving forward since these efforts are still underway. TSA officials acknowledged that the new baseline capability will not address all vulnerabilities identified by TSA, and TSA was not able to provide data or analysis to support its assertion that requiring comparisons beyond the baseline was not warranted. The document notes that false negative incidents may be occurring on domestic flights, and that it is difficult to determine the extent to which domestic air carriers may be failing to identify watch-listed individuals. The document also states that the results of the 2005 special emphasis assessment were not sufficient for a reliable estimate of success rates, and that the findings of the January 2008 special emphasis inspection and May 2008 special emphasis assessment were classified and not independently verified.

audience.text: This report is addressed to congressional committees, including the Senate and House Committees on Appropriations, Commerce, Science, and Transportation, Homeland Security, Judiciary, Oversight and Government Reform, and Transportation and Infrastructure, to support their oversight of TSA's aviation security.
